trading.fsHelp_finalCapital: Capital at the end, positions closed

trading.fsHelp_buyHold: Buy with the initial capital and each deposit (with the entry fee) and never sell. In % of what went in.
trading.fsHelp_sharpe: Mean daily return ÷ deviation, × √365, no risk-free rate. Above 1 is good. Sortino only counts losing days.
trading.fsHelp_maxDrawdown: The largest fall from a peak, at each day's close, without deposits. Calmar is CAGR ÷ this fall.
trading.fsHelp_volatility: Deviation of daily returns × √365 (crypto never closes): how much capital swings in a year
trading.fsHelp_trades: Trades closed in the period (the end closes open ones) and the monthly average
trading.fsHelp_winRate: % of winning trades. Payoff is average win ÷ average loss.
trading.fsHelp_profitFactor: Sum of wins ÷ sum of losses. Above 1 makes money. Expectancy is the average result per trade.
trading.fsHelp_costs: Entry and exit fees, slippage and funding (futures)
trading.fsHelp_timeInMarket: % of the period with at least one open position, and the most open at once
trading.fsHelp_positiveDays: % of days capital went up, without deposits (days with no position count as flat)
trading.fsScoreMeaning_solid: Makes money, holds out of sample and isn't luck: it can move to real money, with little capital
trading.fsScoreMeaning_promising: There's an edge, but the weak points below need work before risking capital
trading.fsScoreMeaning_notReady: The weak points outweigh the edge: don't risk capital on it like this
trading.fsScoreHowIntro: Each part scores 0 to 1 × its weight; the sum is the score. Scales and weights are conventions: leveraged crypto deserves stricter ones.
trading.fsScoreFormula_outOfSample: 50% if the out-of-sample return (last {{pct}}%) is positive ({{ret}}) + 50% × min(PF out {{pfOut}} / PF in {{pfIn}}, 1)
trading.fsScoreFormula_significance: min({{trades}} trades / {{tradesFull}}, 1) × PSR {{psr}} (probability that the true Sharpe is > 0)
trading.fsScoreFormula_stability: R² {{r2}} of the line on log equity: 1 = rises in a straight line
trading.fsScoreHowLabels: 70+ “solid”, 45–69 “promising, with caveats”, below 45 “not ready yet”. Bars: blue from 70%, amber from 40%, orange below.
trading.factsheetEquityInfo: Capital against buy and hold, and the same capital in {{asset}}.
trading.fsEquityNote: Log scale. The orange area is the drawdown (own scale down to {{value}})
trading.fsEquityBaseNote: Capital ÷ asset price. If it falls while capital in {{quote}} rises, you're earning less than the asset
trading.fsUnderwaterNote: Distance to the previous high of the performance index (no deposits)
trading.factsheetReturnsInfo: By month, by horizon, the daily distribution and rolling Sharpe.
trading.fsReturnsNote: Blue positive, orange negative. On the performance index (no deposits); dashed, partial periods
trading.fsReturnsPartial: Partial period: the simulation only covers part
trading.fsHorizonNote: Strategy vs buy & hold over the same interval
trading.fsDistributionNote: Bars = actual; line = normal with the same mean and deviation. Tails above the line = hidden risk
trading.fsRollingSharpeNote: Lines at 0, 1 and 2. A lasting decline is the first sign the edge is fading
trading.fsMonthlyNote: Trades, stops, costs and result per month; the return is equity's (open positions included)
trading.factsheetRiskInfo: How far it can fall, for how long and how fat the tails are, on daily returns.
trading.fsHelp_var95: The 5th percentile of daily returns: one bad day in 20 loses at least this
trading.fsHelp_cvar95: The average of the worst 5% of days (below the 95% VaR): the loss on a really bad day
trading.fsHelp_var99: The 1st percentile of daily returns: the very bad day, one in 100
trading.fsHelp_skewness: Asymmetry of daily returns. Negative: big drops more common than big gains.
trading.fsHelp_kurtosis: Excess kurtosis (a normal has 0). Above 0, more extreme days than a normal.
trading.fsHelp_ulcer: Root of the mean squared daily drawdown: combines depth and time below the peak
trading.fsHelp_pain: Mean daily drawdown: how far below the peak, on average
trading.fsHelp_tailRatio: 95th ÷ 5th percentile (absolute). Above 1, the very good days outweigh the very bad ones.
trading.fsHelp_worstDay: The worst and best day of the run, on the performance index (no deposits)
trading.fsHelp_drawdowns: How often the index fell below its high: each episode runs from a peak until it's regained (or the end)
trading.fsDrawdownsNote: Start, trough, recovery and duration, in days
trading.fsDrawdownsNone: No drawdowns: the index never went below its previous high
trading.factsheetRatiosInfo: Return per unit of risk: these are what you compare strategies with.
trading.fsRatioFormula_omega: Sum of positive days / sum of negative days
trading.fsRatioFormula_gainToPain: Sum of months / sum of monthly losses
trading.fsRatioFormula_profitFactor: Gross profit / gross loss of the trades
trading.fsRatioFormula_sqn: √n × mean / deviation of the return per trade (n up to {{max}})
trading.fsRatioRef_kelly: Use ¼ to ½ of the value
trading.factsheetBenchmarksInfo: Against holding BTC, ETH, half of each and gold. In blue, the best of each column.
trading.fsCaptureNote: Against {{asset}}, in days. Ideally it catches rises and protects in falls
trading.fsCaptureReading_upCapture: How much of the average {{asset}} rise it catches
trading.fsCaptureReading_downCapture: How much of the average {{asset}} fall it takes; lower is better
trading.fsScatterNote: Each dot is a day. The line's slope is the beta ({{beta}})
trading.setupSheetInfo: The full configuration. Results are in the Summary.

trading.shEntriesNote: Enters when → enters at → with how much → exits (whichever comes first)

trading.fsOrdExpiredDetail_other: Price did not get there in {{count}} candles
trading.fsOrdExpiredLate: Price did not get there in time

trading.addValueAreaHint: Close between the previous VAL and VAH (inside), or above VAH or below VAL (outside). Creates the profile if missing.
trading.profileSessionMissing: This exchange doesn't have that part of the day, so the profile would never have sessions. Pick another session or exchange.
trading.profileDevelopingDaily: On daily candles each candle is a session, so there's no developing profile. Use the previous session or a smaller timeframe.
trading.fsProfileInfo: The strategy's volume profile ({{name}}): how sessions open against the previous value area, whether price returns to past POCs and how trades did by where they entered.
trading.fsProfileHelp_sessions: Sessions with a profile and the average value area width (VAH − VAL) as % of price
trading.fsProfileHelp_outside: % of sessions that opened above the previous VAH or below the previous VAL
trading.fsProfileHelp_returned: Of those opening outside, % where price got back into the previous value area that session (and % reaching the POC)
trading.fsProfileHelp_brokeOut: Of those opening inside the previous value area, % where price went past VAH or VAL
trading.fsProfileHelp_naked: % of past POCs price came back to, and the median candles until it did
trading.fsProfileHelp_inside: % of trades entering between the previous session's VAL and VAH
trading.fsProfilePositionTitle: Where it entered against the value area
trading.fsProfilePositionNote: Entry price against the previous session's value area
trading.fsProfileDistanceTitle: Average R by distance to the POC
trading.fsProfileDistanceNote: Distance from entry to the previous session's POC (negative = below). Faded: fewer than {{count}} trades.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileSessions_what: How many sessions had a volume profile in the period (with the session, exchange and rows of the strategy's indicator) and how wide the value area was on average: the distance between VAH and VAL as a % of price.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileSessions_read: A wide value area means sessions with prices spread out (more volatility, levels further apart); a narrow one, sessions packed into a small range. It is a ruler for stops and targets placed at the VAH, VAL or POC.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileOutside_what: The % of sessions that opened outside the previous session's value area — above the VAH or below the VAL —, with how many on each side.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileOutside_read: Opening outside the value area shows price accepted or rejected yesterday's value right away. Many outside opens make return-to-value or breakout strategies more useful; few, those that work inside it.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileOutside_cons:
In a 24-hour market the "open" is just the first candle of the chosen session (in crypto, UTC midnight), not an opening auction like on an exchange.
With few sessions the % changes a lot between simulations.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileReturned_what: Of the sessions that opened outside the previous value area, the % where price re-entered it during the session, and the % where it actually reached the POC.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileReturned_read: This is the profile traders' "80% rule": opening outside and coming back in, price tends to cross the value area to the other side. A high % favours return-to-POC entries; a low %, breakouts that follow through.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileBrokeOut_what: Of the sessions that opened inside the previous value area, the % where price went past the VAH or VAL during the session.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileBrokeOut_read: It shows how often a "balanced" session becomes unbalanced. A high % favours VAH/VAL breakouts; a low %, strategies that buy at the VAL and sell at the VAH.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileNaked_what: For each past session, whether price later touched its POC again (a naked POC stops being naked once a candle touches it), the median candles until that happened and how many are still untouched.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileNaked_read: Naked POCs act as magnets for many traders. A high % with few candles until touched justifies using them as targets; many untouched and long medians say the opposite.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileNaked_cons:
POCs near the end of the period had little time to be touched: they pull the % down.
The median counts candles of the simulation timeframe, not hours.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileInside_what: The % of trades whose entry price was inside the previous session's value area (between the VAL and VAH).
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileInside_read: It says where the strategy usually enters: inside the value accepted yesterday or outside it. Compare with the table next to it to see whether one zone gives better trades.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfilePosition_what: Trades grouped by where the entry price was against the previous session's value area — above the VAH, inside above the POC, inside below the POC, below the VAL —, with each group's win rate, average R and P&L.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfilePosition_read: Look for the zone that pays: if trades above the VAH win and those inside lose, the strategy is a breakout one and gains from an "only outside the value area" filter; the other way round, an "only inside" filter.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfilePosition_cons:
Groups with few trades say little: check the trades column before drawing conclusions.
It counts the previous session's profile, not the developing one, even if the strategy uses the other.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileDistance_what: Trades' average R by the distance (in %) from the entry price to the previous session's POC: negative when it entered below it, positive above.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileDistance_read: It shows whether entering near the POC is better than far from it. Positive bars near 0 favour entries at the POC; positive only far from it, entries after price moved away from value.
trading.fsExplain_entryProfileDistance_cons:
Faded bars have fewer than 5 trades: their average R is very uncertain.
The distance is a % of price, so the same range means more in a calm market than in a volatile one.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterLoss_what: Trades where the last trade to close before their entry lost (P&L of zero or less), from any entry: the average R, win rate and how many there are.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterLoss_read: Compare with the «After a win» card and with the overall average R. If trades after a loss are clearly worse, losses come in clusters (unfavourable market) and a pause or a smaller size after losses («do not trade if», sizing rules) may help. If they are better, cutting size after losses would be a mistake. The «The next trade» table has more cases.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterLoss_cons:
With overlapping positions, the previous trade may be from another entry and unrelated.
Small differences are almost always noise.
Needs a stop for the average R.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterStop_what: What price did 6, 24 and 72 bars after trades that exited through the entry's stop: the average move in the trade's favour (positive = price turned towards the trade after the stop) and the % in which price reached that entry's original take profit during that time (only trades with a take).
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterStop_read: A high «Reached the original take» is the sign of a premature stop: the trade was right but noise took it out. Below 15–20% is normal. If the average move is negative, the stop did its job (price kept going against). Before widening the stop, check the MAE vs result cloud (4.5).
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterStop_cons:
Widening the stop changes the size of losses and positions: this number alone is not enough to decide.
Trades without a take do not count in «Reached the original take».
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterTake_what: What price did 6, 24 and 72 bars (of the timeframe) after trades that exited at take profit: the average move in the trade's favour, from the exit price to that bar's close; the % in which price went a further 2% in favour during that time; and, of those that exited with price on the favourable side, the % in which it came back to the entry price.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterTake_read: A clearly positive average move and a high «Went on +2%» say the take is short: the trade had more to give, and a bigger take, a trailing stop or a partial exit may earn more. If price usually comes back to entry, the take is catching the move well. Compare with «Left on the table» in 4.3.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterTake_cons:
It is what happened afterwards, not what another exit could have captured.
Trades near the end of the period without enough bars are left out.
The 2% is fixed: a lot for a calm asset, little for a very volatile one.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterTrailing_what: What price did 6, 24 and 72 bars after trades that exited by trailing stop: the average move in the trade's favour, the % in which it went a further 2% in favour during that time and, of those that exited with price in favour, the % in which it came back to the entry price.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterTrailing_read: If price keeps going well in favour after exiting, the trailing is tight and cuts trends halfway. If it often comes back to entry, the trailing is protecting profit well. Compare with MFE capture in exit efficiency (4.8): a good trailing leaves little on the table without exiting too early.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterTrailing_cons:
Few trailing exits make the percentages unstable.
Does not show what a wider trailing would have given back before exiting.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterWin_what: Trades where the last trade to close before their entry won (positive P&L), from any entry: the average R, win rate and how many there are.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterWin_read: If trades after a win are better than average, wins come in clusters (trends) and increasing size after wins may pay; if they are worse, the market tends to revert after a good trade. Compare with «After a loss»: only a large difference with many trades deserves a rule.
trading.fsExplain_entryAfterWin_cons:
With overlapping positions, exit order is not decision order.
With few trades, the difference is noise.
trading.fsExplain_entryBest_what: The strategy entry with the largest summed P&L over the whole period, with the average R of its trades below. P&L is net (fees and funding deducted) and each trade's R is that P&L divided by the initial risk (quantity × entry price × distance to the stop that trade had).
trading.fsExplain_entryBest_read: Shows which entry carries the strategy. High P&L with a low average R means many small trades; a high average R with few trades calls for caution. Compare with the «% of profit» column in the table below and with the «In» and «Out» R: the best entry is only trustworthy if it also wins out of sample.
trading.fsExplain_entryBreakEvens_what: How many trades exited at break-even: the stop moved to the entry price (by the entry's break-even or by a stop adjustment) and price came back to it.
trading.fsExplain_entryBreakEvens_read: Many break-evens with few takes means the stop moves up too early and takes out trades that would later go your way; check 4.4 and exit efficiency (4.8). Few or none is normal if break-even is far away or off. A break-even exits near zero but with fees it is usually a small loss.
trading.fsExplain_entryCapture_what: Of the summed MFE (each trade's best favourable move, in % of entry price) of the trades that were ever in profit, the part the exit captured: the sum of price moves up to the exit divided by the sum of MFE. Summing before dividing stops trades that barely moved from blowing up the average.
trading.fsExplain_entryCapture_read: Above 50% is very good; 25–50% is typical; near 0 or negative means that, together, trades give back almost all (or more) of what they had gained. Low capture with many takes points to distant takes; with many stops, to trades that were winning and turned. See exit efficiency by group (table below) and «Left on the table» in 4.3.
trading.fsExplain_entryCapture_pros:
Measures exit quality in a single number.
Independent of position size.
trading.fsExplain_entryCapture_cons:
Uses the price move, without fees or funding.
Nobody exits at the best point: 100% is impossible in practice.
It can improve just by exiting early, at the cost of trades that would go much further.
trading.fsExplain_entryCorrelation_what: The Pearson correlation between the weekly P&L of each pair of entries (weeks Monday to Sunday in UTC, each trade in the week it closed, weeks without trades at 0), in a heatmap from −1 to 1. Empty when an entry does not vary.
trading.fsExplain_entryCorrelation_read: Near 0 or negative, the entries win and lose at different times and diversify the risk: the whole is more stable than each one. Above 0.6–0.7 they are practically the same bet and adding risk to both is concentrating it. Cross-check with the per-entry equity (4.1) and the risk schemes above.
trading.fsExplain_entryCorrelation_cons:
Weeks without trades count as 0 and pull the correlation towards 0 for entries that trade little.
Measures only linear, average relationships; correlations usually rise in crises.
By exit week: long trades fall into a single week.
trading.fsExplain_entryDurations_what: Trades grouped by the number of bars they were open (1–2, 3–6, 7–12, 13–24, 25–48, 49–96, 97–192 and more than 192, only the buckets with trades): trades, win rate, expectancy (average P&L), average R, % of entry stops and P&L.
trading.fsExplain_entryDurations_read: Shows whether time in the trade relates to the result. Short trades are often stops and long ones the winners; if very long trades lose, the strategy gets stuck in directionless positions and a time exit (maxBars) may help. Cross-check with the average R path (4.8) and the bars to stop.
trading.fsExplain_entryEfficiency_what: By group of trades (all, winners, losers, each entry and each exit): trades, average MFE and average MAE (the best and worst move during the trade, in % of entry price), MFE capture (sum of moves up to the exit ÷ sum of MFE, for trades with MFE) and the average bars to the best and worst point.
trading.fsExplain_entryEfficiency_read: For winners, low capture points to late exits (profit comes back before exiting) or distant takes. For losers, the average MFE tells how far in profit those trades got: a high MFE among losers calls for a break-even or a stop adjustment. By exit, compare which one makes the most of the move. Negative capture = the group gave back more than it ever had.
trading.fsExplain_entryEfficiency_cons:
Price move, without fees or funding.
Losers and winners are split by final result, which exaggerates the differences.
Small groups have unstable values.
trading.fsExplain_entryEquity_what: The cumulative P&L of each entry over time, in the quote currency: one line per entry that only changes when one of its trades closes (hence the steps), from the start to the end of the simulation.
trading.fsExplain_entryEquity_read: A good entry rises steadily; one that only won in a single episode shows as a jump followed by a flat or falling line. Look for entries that stopped rising in the final part (it may be the out-of-sample part, see 3.1) and entries that rise when others fall (they diversify, see the correlation in 4.6).
trading.fsExplain_entryEquity_cons:
It is realised P&L: it does not show drawdowns while trades are open.
In absolute amounts, without adjusting for capital growth (with compounding, recent trades weigh more).
With many entries, the lines overlap.
trading.fsExplain_entryExitMix_what: The percentage of each entry's trades that exited through each exit (the same columns as the matrix above). Each row adds up to 100%.
trading.fsExplain_entryExitMix_read: Shows each entry's profile: one that almost always exits at the stop lives on a few large takes; one that exits mostly by time or at the end of the period may not have well-defined exits. Compare entries: if one has many more stops than the others with the same stop, its signal is weaker. Combine with the matrix P&L to see whether the most frequent exit is the one that pays.
trading.fsExplain_entryExitReasons_what: One row per exit (the 4.2 columns): trades, win rate, average and total P&L, average bars open and «Left on the table»: the average MFE (the best favourable move during the trade, in % of the entry price) minus the average price move up to the exit.
trading.fsExplain_entryExitReasons_read: See which exits pay and which cost. A high «Left on the table» on a take means price used to go much further before coming back; on a stop it is natural (they are trades that were winning and ended losing). A condition exit with negative P&L and a lot left on the table is exiting late. Compare with exit efficiency (4.8).
trading.fsExplain_entryExitReasons_cons:
MFE is the best moment, which nobody catches every time: some profit left on the table is unavoidable.
The move is price only, without fees or funding, while P&L includes them.
trading.fsExplain_entryFlips_what: How many entries have a positive average R in one part of the sample and a negative one in the other. The split is the one from 3.1: at the configured out-of-sample share or, without it, at the last 30% of the period, at UTC midnight, and each trade belongs to the part where it was entered.
trading.fsExplain_entryFlips_read: Ideally 0. An entry that wins inside and loses outside was probably fitted to the past (overfitting) or stopped working; one that loses inside and wins outside is not trustworthy either. See which ones in the «In» and «Out» columns of the table below and cross-check with 3.1.
trading.fsExplain_entryFlips_cons:
With few trades in one of the parts, the sign of R changes by chance.
Needs a stop (without one there is no R and the entry does not count).
It does not tell a change from +0.01R to −0.01R apart from a large drop.
trading.fsExplain_entryGroups_what: Trades in three splits: pyramid position (1st = no other open from the same entry, 2nd = with one, 3rd or more), order type (market, limit level — in favour of price, without slippage — or stop level — breakout) and the first trade of the day (UTC, by entry) against the following ones that day. For each group: trades, win rate, average R, P&L, % of stops and bars. Only groups with trades appear.
trading.fsExplain_entryGroups_read: In the pyramid, later positions with worse R say that pyramiding adds risk without return. For order types, compare limit and stop orders with market ones (and with 2.3, orders and execution price). If later trades in the day are worse than the first, a daily trade limit may help.
trading.fsExplain_entryGroups_cons:
Each group mixes different entries: an entry with many trades dominates.
The day is in UTC, not in the simulation's time zone.
Groups with few trades are unstable.
trading.fsExplain_entryJournal_what: The simulation's saved trades, from most recent to oldest (20 on screen, all of them with the pager under «See all»): number, entry, side, entry time and price, exit time and reason (with partials and scale-ins), exit price, initial quantity, bars, MAE and MFE (in % of entry price), fees, funding, net result, % on margin and capital after the trade. Dates in UTC.
trading.fsExplain_entryJournal_read: Use it to look at concrete trades: confirm the strategy does what was expected, find anomalous trades (losses much larger than the stop, heavy funding, a large MFE that ended in a loss) and follow capital trade by trade. Cross-check with the simulation chart to see the trade on the candles.
trading.fsExplain_entryKelly_what: Per entry, using only trades inside the sample: win rate, payoff (average win ÷ average loss), Kelly (W − (1 − W) ÷ payoff, the fraction of capital that maximises long-run growth), ¼ Kelly (between 0 and 2%), the proportional to expectancy in R (the average of the positive entries = 1%, up to 2%) and the suggestion: up to ¼ Kelly, at most 1.5%; with negative Kelly, turn off or review.
trading.fsExplain_entryKelly_read: Negative Kelly means that, with these numbers, the entry loses in the long run. Full Kelly is too aggressive in practice (drawdowns are huge and the estimates carry error), so ¼ is used. More than 2% risk per trade rarely pays. The suggestion feeds the schemes in the table above: confirm there, in the out-of-sample part, whether it works.
trading.fsExplain_entryKelly_pros:
Turns win rate and payoff into a well-founded risk size.
Computed inside the sample, without using the part that serves as a test.
The caps (¼, 2%, 1.5%) prevent oversized positions.
trading.fsExplain_entryKelly_cons:
Kelly assumes win rate and payoff are known and stable; with few trades the error is large.
Ignores correlation between entries and simultaneous positions.
Payoff comes from P&L in money, not R: it depends on the size each trade had.
trading.fsExplain_entryLosing_what: How many entries finished the whole period with negative (net) P&L, out of all the strategy's entries. An entry with no trades does not count as losing.
trading.fsExplain_entryLosing_read: Ideally 0. A losing entry inside a profitable set is being paid for by the others: check the «Out» R and the «Without this entry» column in the table below. If more than half the entries lose, profit is concentrated and the strategy is fragile.
trading.fsExplain_entryMae_what: One point per trade: on the horizontal axis the MAE (maximum adverse excursion, the worst price was against the trade while open, in % of the entry price, checked on minutes) and on the vertical axis the result (net P&L in % of the entry value). Blue won, red lost. The result axis goes up to the 98th percentile with some headroom, so one huge trade does not squash the rest.
trading.fsExplain_entryMae_read: If almost all winners stay in a narrow MAE band (for example, never beyond −1.5%) and the stop is far beyond it, the stop can be tightened without losing winners. Winners that went far against you (blue points on the left) show that a shorter stop would have cut them. Losers that barely went against you and still lost exited for another reason (time, condition).
trading.fsExplain_entryMae_pros:
The classic tool for tuning stop distance.
Shows the noise that winners usually endure.
trading.fsExplain_entryMae_cons:
MAE comes from minutes and ignores when it happened (early or late in the trade).
Changing the stop changes position size and the following trades: the cloud does not simulate that.
The few trades above the 98th percentile are left out of the drawing.
trading.fsExplain_entryMatrix_what: A heatmap with entries in the rows and exits in the columns (each stop, take, trailing, break-even, condition exit, time exit, stop adjustment, etc., with its value; equal stops of different entries share a column). Each cell shows the trades and win rate of that pair; the colour is the average P&L per trade and the total appears in the tooltip.
trading.fsExplain_entryMatrix_read: Green cells are the paths that make money, red ones the paths that cost. In a healthy strategy the take and favourable exits are green and the stop is red but small. A condition exit that is always red may be cutting good trades too early; compare with «Left on the table» in 4.3 and with exit efficiency (4.8).
trading.fsExplain_entryMatrix_cons:
Cells with 1 or 2 trades have strong colours and little meaning.
The colour is average P&L, which depends on position size.
It does not say whether the exit came early or late (that is in 4.4 and 4.8).
trading.fsExplain_entryNextTrade_what: How a trade behaves depending on those that closed before its entry (from any entry, in exit order): after a win, a loss, an entry stop, two wins in a row and two losses in a row. For each case: trades, win rate, average R, P&L and the probability of repeating (winning again, losing again or being stopped again).
trading.fsExplain_entryNextTrade_read: If the probability of repeating is similar to the overall rate (the strategy's win rate or % of stops), trades are independent and streak-based rules do not help. If after two losses the next one is clearly worse, losses cluster and a pause («do not trade if») may pay; if it is better, cutting size after losses gives up profit. With sizing rules on, P&L reflects them.
trading.fsExplain_entryNextTrade_cons:
With overlapping positions, the previous trade may be unrelated to the next.
The two-in-a-row cases have few trades.
P&L is affected by sizing rules; average R is not.
trading.fsExplain_entryPeak_what: The average number of bars from the entry bar to the bar where the trade was at its best price (the MFE minute), in the simulation's timeframe. Below, the average number of bars trades stay open.
trading.fsExplain_entryPeak_read: If the best point comes long before the exit (for example, 5 bars out of 30), trades spend most of their time giving back profit: a trailing, a partial exit or a time exit may help. If the best point is near the end, the exit is well synchronised with the move. Cross-check with the average R path (chart below).
trading.fsExplain_entryPerformance_what: One row per entry: side, trades, win rate, payoff (average win ÷ average loss), profit factor, expectancy (average P&L per trade), average R, net P&L, «% of profit» (its share of total P&L), average bars open, «% stops» (only the entry's stop, without trailing or adjustments), the average R «In» and «Out» the sample (the 3.1 split, by entry) and «Without this entry»: the strategy's return run in the engine without it.
trading.fsExplain_entryPerformance_read: Look for entries with PF above 1 (above 1.5 is good), positive expectancy and R and, above all, positive R «Out» too. A low win rate is not bad if the payoff is high. If «Without this entry» is higher than the current return, the entry is hurting the whole. Cross-check with the entry → exit matrix (4.2) to see how each one exits.
trading.fsExplain_entryPerformance_cons:
Entries with few trades have very unstable numbers.
R needs a stop; without one the R columns are empty.
P&L and «% of profit» depend on each entry's size, not only on the signal.
trading.fsExplain_entryRDist_what: The histogram of each trade's result in R (net P&L divided by the trade's initial risk, quantity × entry price × distance to the stop), in 0.25R bars between −3R and 6R; those beyond the limits go into the edge bars. Trades without a stop have no R and are left out.
trading.fsExplain_entryRDist_read: In a strategy with a stop, a spike near −1R is normal (the stops, slightly below because of fees and slippage). What pays the system is the right tail: trades of 2R, 3R or more. Many trades below −1R point to gaps or slippage (see «Extra cost at the stop»). A distribution with only small wins and −1R losses needs a high win rate.
trading.fsExplain_entryRDist_cons:
Needs a stop on every entry to be complete.
Clips at the edges: a 20R trade shows in the 6R bar.
Does not show trade order or streaks.
trading.fsExplain_entryScaleIns_what: One row per scale-in of each entry: the rule spelled out; «Reached», the times price (or the conditions) got to the scale-in before the exit; «Filled», those that added quantity (and how many were smaller than requested, for lack of capital); «No capital», those that did not fit in free capital; «Below minimum», those rejected by the minimum quantity or value; trades with this scale-in against those with none (average R on initial risk · win rate (trades)); and the strategy run without the scale-in: trades, return and max DD «without the rule» and «Adds» (current return minus return without it, in p.p.).
trading.fsExplain_entryScaleIns_read: Look first at «Adds» and «Max DD without the rule»: a scale-in that adds little and greatly increases max drawdown does not pay. If «No capital» is high, the initial size already uses all the capital and the scale-in almost never fills; lower the size per trade to test it properly. Trades with a scale-in are, by nature, trades that went in favour: their R is better by selection, not necessarily because of the scale-in.
trading.fsExplain_entryScaleIns_pros:
Measures each scale-in's real contribution, with the engine.
Shows whether the scale-in can actually fill (capital, minimums).
Combines return and risk in the «without the rule» columns.
trading.fsExplain_entryScaleIns_cons:
A single run: small differences in «Adds» may be noise.
R is on initial risk: a scale-in increases the position's real risk without showing in R.
The with/without comparison has selection bias.
trading.fsExplain_entrySchemes_what: Six per-entry risk schemes run in the engine, each with every entry sized by risk (the % of capital lost if the stop is hit; 0% = off) and without the sizing rules: equal for all (1%), only the positive ones, proportional to expectancy in R (max 2%), ¼ Kelly (max 2%), turn off the worst, and double the best with zero on the worst. Risks are chosen only from trades inside the sample (the Kelly table below); the table gives trades, return, max DD and Calmar over the whole period and, out of sample, the return, PF and Δ in p.p. against equal for all.
trading.fsExplain_entrySchemes_read: The out-of-sample columns are the ones that count, because the schemes were chosen without seeing that part. A scheme that improves the total return but not outside is overfitted. Look for a positive outside Δ with a similar or smaller max DD. If the «Scale-ins without capital» column appears, risk sizing is using all the capital and scale-ins no longer fit.
trading.fsExplain_entrySchemes_pros:
Tests capital allocation across entries without looking ahead.
Runs each scheme in the engine, with the real interactions between entries.
Compares against a neutral reference (equal for all).
trading.fsExplain_entrySchemes_cons:
Needs a stop on every entry.
A single inside/outside split: the outside result can be luck, especially with few trades.
Removes the strategy's sizing rules, so it does not compare with the current setup.
trading.fsExplain_entrySecond_what: Trades opened when there was already exactly one open position from the same entry (the 2nd pyramid position, with maxPositions above 1): the average R, how many there are and the P&L they made.
trading.fsExplain_entrySecond_read: Compare the average R with that of the 1st position («Pyramid, order type and order in the day» table, below). If the 2nd position has an equal or better average R, pyramiding adds profit; if it is worse or negative, it is adding risk to late entries and lowering the entry's maxPositions may improve the whole. Without pyramiding, the card is empty.
trading.fsExplain_entrySecond_cons:
The 2nd position opens at a different moment from the 1st: it compares different signals, not only the pyramid effect.
It usually has few trades.
trading.fsExplain_entrySeparation_what: Bar by bar since entry, the average R of trades that end up winning and of those that end up losing (at each bar's close while open, the final R after they exit). It is the first bar where the winners' curve is more than 0.5R above the losers'. Only trades with a stop, up to 500 bars.
trading.fsExplain_entrySeparation_read: Until that bar, a winning and a losing trade cannot be told apart. After it, a trade that is not yet in favour is very likely a loser: that is where a time exit (maxBars) or a stop adjustment makes sense. A very late or missing separation means the result is decided late or that exits are almost random. See the average path chart below.
trading.fsExplain_entrySeparation_cons:
Needs a stop (without R there are no curves).
The 0.5R is a fixed threshold.
Because it mixes trades that already exited (with their final R), the losers' curve drops early because of stops.
trading.fsExplain_entrySides_what: The number of buy (long) and sell (short) trades in the period, adding up the entries of each direction.
trading.fsExplain_entrySides_read: Shows which way the strategy bets. A long-only strategy in a market that rose a lot may win just because of that: compare the return with buy & hold (1.1) and with market regimes (3.6). With a strong imbalance, check the per-entry table to see whether the minority side wins.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopExtra_what: On average, how much worse the stops' exit price was than the stop level, in % of that level. It combines the configured slippage and gaps: when the minute already opens beyond the stop, the exit is at that price and not at the level.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopExtra_read: Close to 0% (or equal to the configured slippage) is expected. Values well above point to markets with gaps or stops that hit at very volatile moments; in that case the real loss of a stop is larger than −1R. Cross-check with the gaps in 5.9 and the cost stress in 3.5.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopExtra_cons:
It is an average: a single huge gap is diluted.
Slippage is a configured estimate, not the real order book.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopRules_what: One row per stop adjustment of each entry (the rules «from when the stop moves to…»): the rule spelled out; «Happened», the trades where it triggered before the exit and the % of the entry's trades; «Exited on it», those that closed at the stop it set (average R · win rate (trades)) and the P&L of those exits; trades with and without the adjustment; and the strategy run again in the engine without that adjustment: «Trades without the rule», «Return without the rule» and «Max DD without the rule». «Adds» is the current return minus the return without the adjustment, in p.p.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopRules_read: The decisive column is «Adds»: positive (green), the adjustment adds return to the strategy; negative, the strategy would earn more without it. Combine with «Max DD without the rule»: an adjustment that adds little but clearly reduces max drawdown may be worth it. «Trades with it» against «Trades without it» proves nothing alone, because adjustments that trigger on profit only happen in trades that already went in favour.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopRules_pros:
Measures the real effect of each adjustment with the engine, including later trades and capital.
Shows how often the adjustment acts and how the trades where it acted exit.
The «without the rule» columns compare return and risk side by side.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopRules_cons:
It is a single run over the same period: a small difference in «Adds» may be noise.
Removing a rule changes the whole sequence of trades (capital, free positions), not only the trades where it acted.
The with/without comparison has selection bias.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopStreak_what: The longest run of consecutive stops, in the order trades exited. Any other exit (take, trailing, condition, etc.) breaks the run.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopStreak_read: It is the worst psychological and capital moment the strategy had. Multiply by the risk per trade to estimate the drawdown (10 stops at 1% ≈ −10%). Compare with the streak distribution in the «Stops per month and streaks» chart and with Monte Carlo ruin (3.2): the real streak is just one of many possible, and it can be longer in the future.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopTime_what: The average number of bars from the entry bar to the stop bar, in the simulation's timeframe (at least 1). Only trades that exited through the entry's stop.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopTime_read: Very fast stops (1 to 3 bars) point to entries at bad moments or a stop inside the bar's normal noise. Compare with the trades' total bars (the «Bars to the best point» card) and with the average R path (4.8): if losers reveal themselves early, a time exit can cut losses before the stop.
trading.fsExplain_entryStops_what: How many trades exited through the entry's stop loss and the percentage of all trades. Only the original stop counts: trailing, break-even and stops moved by an adjustment (4.9) are counted separately.
trading.fsExplain_entryStops_read: A trend-following strategy usually has 50% to 70% stops and wins on the few takes; a mean-reversion one usually has fewer. The number alone is neither good nor bad: cross-check with «Stops that reversed» and with 4.4 to see whether the stop is too tight, and with the R distribution (4.5).
trading.fsExplain_entryStopsMonth_what: At the top, bars with the entry's stops in each month (UTC, by exit day, including months with none) and the line of the monthly average. At the bottom, how many times there were runs of 1, 2, 3… consecutive stops, in exit order.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopsMonth_read: Months with many more stops than average show periods when the market did not suit the strategy; cross-check with regimes (3.6) and the calendar (5.5). In the streak histogram, a long tail (runs of 6, 8, 10) tells how much capital is needed to survive bad spells and whether a pause rule is worth it.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopsOfLosses_what: Of the losing trades (P&L of zero or less), the percentage that exited through the entry's stop loss. The rest lost through another exit (condition, time, trailing, opposite signal, end of period) before reaching the stop.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopsOfLosses_read: Close to 100%, the stop is the only defence and losses are all around −1R. Lower, the other exits are cutting losses earlier, which is good if the small losses make up for the trades that would have recovered. Compare with the «% stops» column in the per-entry table and with the −1R spike in 4.5.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopsOfLosses_cons:
Trades that exited near zero with fees count as losses.
Does not show the size of the losses that were not stops.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopsReversed_what: The percentage of stops where, in the 48 hours after the exit, price reached that entry's take profit (checked minute by minute on highs and lows). Only stops of trades with a take count; the detail says how many there were.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopsReversed_read: Below 15–20% is normal. A high percentage points to a stop that is too tight: the trade was right, but noise took it out first. Before widening the stop, check «Reached the original take» at 6, 24 and 72 bars in 4.4 and the MAE vs result cloud (4.5) to see whether winners usually go far against you.
trading.fsExplain_entryStopsReversed_cons:
Widening the stop also increases each stop's loss: a high number does not guarantee that widening pays.
The fixed 48 h window does not depend on the timeframe.
Trades without a take are left out.
trading.fsExplain_entryTakes_what: How many trades exited at the take profit and the percentage of all trades.
trading.fsExplain_entryTakes_read: Together with stops it gives the strategy's balance: few takes need to be large (high payoff) to pay for the stops. If takes are rare and 4.4 shows that price usually keeps going your way after them, the take may be short; if it is almost never hit, it may be too far and trades end up exiting another way.
trading.fsExplain_entryTradePath_what: At each bar since entry, the average unrealised R of trades that ended up winning, of those that ended up losing and of all of them (at the bar's close while open; after they exit, the final R counts). It goes up to the 75th percentile of bars open (between 10 and 500 bars) and always past the separation bar, which is marked. Only trades with a stop.
trading.fsExplain_entryTradePath_read: The winners' curve should move away from the losers' early. If losers stay near 0R for a long time before dropping to −1R, there is wasted time that a time exit could cut. If the winners' curve rises and then falls, trades give back profit (see MFE capture). The all-trades curve shows the expected average gain at each bar.
trading.fsExplain_entryTradePath_pros:
Shows how a typical trade evolves, not only how it ends.
Helps choose time exits and stop adjustments.
trading.fsExplain_entryTradePath_cons:
Splitting by final result is looking ahead: live, you do not know which curve you are on.
Only bar closes, not what happened inside them.
Needs a stop on every entry to include all trades.
trading.fsExplain_entryWithoutWorst_what: The strategy's net return when run again in the engine without the worst entry (the one with the lowest P&L), against the current return with all of them. It is not a subtraction: without that entry, the others get the free capital and positions and may open trades that did not fit before.
trading.fsExplain_entryWithoutWorst_read: If the value is higher than the current one (green), the strategy earns more without that entry. Before turning it off, check whether it also loses out of sample («Out» column in the table) and whether the difference is large; a small improvement may be noise. Only exists in strategies with more than one entry.
trading.fsExplain_entryWithoutWorst_cons:
Picking the worst by looking at the whole period is looking ahead: the gain tends to be optimistic.
One more simulation over the same period: it does not prove the improvement holds.
trading.fsExplain_entryWorst_what: The entry with the smallest summed P&L over the whole period (net of fees and funding) and the average R of its trades. It only appears when more than one entry has trades.
trading.fsExplain_entryWorst_read: If P&L is negative, this entry is taking money from the others. See the «Turn off the worst» card and the «Without this entry» column in the table to know what the strategy would do without it, and the «Out» R to see whether the loss repeats out of sample. A worst entry that is still positive is not a problem, just the weakest.
trading.fsExplain_hoursBest_what: The entry hour with the largest summed net P&L (after fees and funding) and the win rate of the trades opened in it.
trading.fsExplain_hoursBest_read: Check whether the result comes from many trades or from one or two big ones: cross it with the trade count in the 5.1 table and with 5.8, which tests whether the best hours stay good out of sample. A low win rate with high P&L means a few large wins.
trading.fsExplain_hoursBusiest_what: The local hour (in the simulation's time zone, with daylight saving) in which the most trades opened, with the count and its share of the total. Each trade counts by the hour it entered, all entries together.
trading.fsExplain_hoursBusiest_read: Shows where the strategy concentrates. An hour holding 20 to 30% of the trades means the signal depends on a moment of the day, such as a session open. Check in the 5.1 table whether that hour also pays: many entries do not mean good results.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalBest_what: The local day the equity rose most, with the stops and trades closed that day. With no closed trades, it was an open position gaining value.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalBest_read: Compare it with total profit: if the best day is a large share, the result depends on few days. See the best days list, with the % of profit, and the concentration test in the verdict.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalBestDays_what: The 12 best local days by equity, with the trades and stops closed, the P&L, the % of total profit that day contributes and the entries of the trades closed on it.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalBestDays_read: Add up the % of the top days: if 3 or 4 days make half the profit, the result depends on rare events and is fragile (the verdict tests the concentration of the 5 best days). A list spread across many months is a good sign.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalLossStreak_what: The longest run of consecutive local days with the equity falling, and how many days had 2 or more stops.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalLossStreak_read: Imagine living through that run: this is where good strategies get switched off. The Monte Carlo in 3.2 shows worse ones are possible. Many days with 2 or more stops suggest bad entries repeated on the same day; a «do not trade if» rule on stops per day may help.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalSplit_what: The days the equity rose and the days it fell, with open positions marked at the local midnight price and without deposits. The % is of days with movement: below 0.005 in absolute terms a day counts as flat.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalSplit_read: Many profitable strategies have fewer than 50% positive days and win through the size of the good days. Compare with the best and worst day and with the daily return distribution in 1.3.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalStopDays_what: The 12 local days with the most stop losses (by the day they closed), from most to fewest, with the closed trades, the day's P&L (from equity) and the entries hit and how many times.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalStopDays_read: Look for patterns in the dates: the same weekday, a particular month, news days. If one entry keeps repeating, it is the problem; if several appear on the same day, entries are firing together on the same move (see the correlation in 4.6).
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalTradeDays_what: How many calendar days (in the simulation's local time) had at least one closed trade, out of all days in the period, and the %.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalTradeDays_read: A low % means a selective strategy with many idle days; a high % means an almost daily strategy. It shows the real frequency and how long you may go without anything happening.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalWinStreak_what: The longest run of consecutive local days with the equity rising; a flat or negative day breaks the run.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalWinStreak_read: Long runs are pleasant but say little on their own; compare with the longest losing run beside it. A large gap in favour of wins is a good sign; the opposite calls for mental preparation.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalWorst_what: The local day the equity fell most, with the stops and trades closed on it.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalWorst_read: The worst pain of a single day: ask yourself whether you could watch the account drop this much. If it is much larger than the risk per trade, losses pile up on the same day (several stops, gaps or positions without a stop): cross it with the days with most stops and with 5.9.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalendar_what: Each local day's P&L in a calendar, one year at a time: rows Monday to Sunday, columns by week; blue gained, orange lost, grey flat. The day's P&L is the equity change (open positions included, no deposits), with the same scale in every year up to the 95th percentile of absolute days, in five bands the legend filters.
trading.fsExplain_hoursCalendar_read: Look for whole orange months (phases where the strategy does not work) and whether good days spread out or cluster. Choose the year above; years are comparable because the scale is the same. Clicking a legend band shows or hides those days, for example only the big losses.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayBest_what: The entry day with the largest summed net P&L, with the average R of the trades opened on it (only those with a stop).
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayBest_read: Average R tells you whether the day is good per trade or just has more trades: if it is similar to other days, the difference is volume. Confirm in the 5.3 table and the 5.4 map.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayBusiest_what: The weekday (by local opening day) with the most trades opened and the average per day: trades divided by the number of days of that kind in the period.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayBusiest_read: The per-day average is fairer than the total when the period does not hold the same number of each weekday. Large differences between days mean the signal depends on the weekly rhythm, for example more volatility mid-week.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayEntries_what: The trades opened on each weekday (local day, Monday to Sunday), stacked by entry, with the total on top.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayEntries_read: See whether any entry only works on certain days or whether volume drops at the weekend. A flat profile means the signal does not depend on the day; a day with many more trades is worth checking in the table for whether it also pays more.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayEntryPnl_what: The summed net P&L of each entry on each weekday (by opening day), in the quote currency; down is a loss. Days without trades for the entry are empty.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayEntryPnl_read: The money summary of the two previous charts. An entry negative on one day and positive on the others suggests a schedule just for it (per-entry schedule, 5.6), as long as it has enough trades on that day.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayEntryStops_what: For each entry and weekday (by opening day), the number of trades closed at the stop loss, as side-by-side bars.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayEntryStops_read: Look for an entry with a spike of stops on a day where the others have none. Compare with the wins chart that follows: many stops with many wins on the same day is just volume.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayEntryWins_what: For each entry and weekday (by opening day), the number of trades closed with positive P&L, whatever the exit.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayEntryWins_read: Read it together with the stops: the ratio of wins to stops on a day says more than either number alone. An entry with no wins on a day it trades is a candidate for a schedule that excludes that day.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayLegend_what: The shared legend of the three per-entry charts that follow (stops, wins and P&L of each entry on each weekday). Each button is an entry; a click hides or shows it in all three at once.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayLegend_read: Hide the entries you do not need so you can compare two or three at a time. Look for an entry that concentrates stops or losses on a day when the others do not: that entry's schedule then fixes it without touching the rest.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayPnl_what: The summed net P&L of the trades opened on each weekday, in the quote currency, blue up and orange down. Days with fewer than 5 trades are faded; the tooltip gives trades, win rate and average R.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayPnl_read: Look for a day clearly out of pattern with enough trades. Small differences between days are normal and do not justify filters. A negative day with average R near zero is more noise than pattern.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayPnl_cons:
A sum: favours days with more trades.
A short period has few weekends.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayStopRate_what: The weekday with the highest % of trades opened on it that closed at the stop loss, with the number of stops.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayStopRate_read: Compare the % with the strategy's average: only a clear gap (10 p.p. or more) with enough trades deserves attention. Check that day's P&L in the cards beside it and in the table before concluding: many stops with large gains on other trades can still be profitable.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayStopsChart_what: Two bars per day: the stops of trades opened that day (by entry day) and the stops hit that day (by exit day, whatever the entry day).
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayStopsChart_read: If on a day the hits far exceed the opened ones (Monday, for example), trades from other days are being swept on that day, typical of the weekend crossing. Similar bars mean trades close on the same day.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayTable_what: One row per day (by local opening day): trades and trades per day (divided by the days of that kind in the period), win rate, stops and %, stops hit that day, P&L, expectancy (average P&L), average R, average bars, the worst run of consecutive stops among that day's trades, and the best and worst entry by P&L.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayTable_read: Expectancy and average R compare days fairly. The worst run shows how much consecutive pain a day can bring: 5 or more stops in a row on the same weekday need attention. The best and worst entry tell whether a day's problem comes from a single entry, fixed in its own schedule (5.6).
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayWeek_what: The net P&L of the trades opened Monday to Friday (local day), with the trades, win rate and % closed at the stop loss.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayWeek_read: Compare with the weekend card: if the week makes almost the whole result, the strategy may skip weekends (5.8 tests «Weekdays only» and 5.9 closing before the weekend). Similar win rate and stop % in both mean the signal does not change.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayWeekend_what: The net P&L of the trades opened on Saturday and Sunday (local day), with the trades, win rate and stop %.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayWeekend_read: In crypto the weekend has less volume and more false moves; a lower win rate or more stops than during the week confirm it. If the weekend loses, test «Weekdays only» in 5.8 and the session rules in 5.9.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayWorst_what: The entry day with the smallest summed net P&L, with the average R of the trades opened on it.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDayWorst_read: A clearly negative average R, with enough trades, suggests entering on that day is bad; 5.8 tests blocking the worst day and shows whether the effect holds out of sample. A worst day with positive P&L means every day wins.
trading.fsExplain_hoursDurationDay_what: Per local entry day: the trades, average bars held and the average duration to each exit type that occurred (stop loss, take profit, trailing, break-even, conditional exit, time).
trading.fsExplain_hoursDurationDay_read: Very different durations between days, especially Friday, point to trades crossing the weekend. If stops arrive much faster than takes, the market turns against you quickly; if they arrive slowly, the idea takes long to fail.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEdges_what: For each exchange (Sydney, Tokyo, London, New York, in UTC hours), the trades opened in the first hour, the last hour and the rest of the session: trades, P&L and stop % of each part.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEdges_read: Opens and closes concentrate volume and false moves. A clearly higher stop % in the first hour suggests waiting for the open to settle; a better P&L at the open means the strategy lives off that impulse.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEdges_cons:
One hour per exchange: few trades.
Fixed UTC hours, without daylight saving.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEmpty_what: How many of the 24 local hours had no entry at all, and which. An empty hour may come from blocked times, an entry's own schedule, or the signal never appearing in it.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEmpty_read: With a schedule configured, the empty hours should match it; unexpected empty hours mean the signal depends on something that only happens at certain times (an opening level, for instance). Zero empty hours = the strategy trades around the clock.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntries_what: The trades opened in each local hour (0h to 23h), stacked by entry, each in its own colour, with the total shown on top. The hour is the entry hour, in the simulation's time zone.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntries_read: See which entries dominate each hour and whether any fires only in one part of the day. A profile concentrated in one or two hours is fragile; a flat profile means the signal does not depend on the hour. The legend hides entries so you can compare them.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryBest_what: The local entry hour with this entry's largest summed net P&L, and the win rate in it.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryBest_read: A starting point for a schedule: if the best hour sits inside a good block (table below), the effect is more credible than a lone hour. Check on the chart how many trades support it.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryBlocks_what: One row per entry and one column per 4-hour local block (00h–03h, 04h–07h…): in each cell trades and win rate on top and P&L below; the colour is the expectancy (average P&L), orange to blue, up to the largest absolute expectancy. At the end, each entry's best and worst block by P&L. Fewer than 5 trades is faded.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryBlocks_read: Blocks pool 4 hours of sample and are sturdier than single hours. Look for entries with a clearly orange block and enough trades: that is where a per-entry schedule makes sense.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryBlocks_cons:
Fixed blocks can cut a session in half.
Colour is relative to the largest cell, which may be extreme.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryBusiest_what: The local hour in which this entry opened the most trades, and how many.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryBusiest_read: Tells you where this entry's signal appears most. Compare with the most-stopped hour in the card beside it: if they match, the entry concentrates its risk where it trades most.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryProfile_what: One panel per entry: its configured schedule (or «no schedule»), trades, stops, side and order type, and bars by local entry hour stacked by outcome — closed in profit (not at a stop), stop loss or other exit. The grey band marks the hours the entry's schedule allows.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryProfile_read: Check whether the entry fires where you expected and whether stops concentrate at specific hours. Hours inside the band with only stops suggest narrowing that entry's schedule (Strategy › Entries › Schedule). The 3 cards below summarise the busiest, best and most-stopped hour.
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryStops_what: The local entry hour in which this entry took the most stop losses, with that hour's stops and trades (on a tie, the one with the higher stop %).
trading.fsExplain_hoursEntryStops_read: If the stops are almost all of that hour's trades, removing it from the entry's schedule is a natural candidate. If it is just the busiest hour, it is volume, not a problem.
trading.fsExplain_hoursExitReasons_what: The trades closed in each local hour, stacked by exit reason: stop loss, trailing, break-even, take profit, conditional exit, time and, when present, liquidation, opposite signal, excluded period and end. The hour is the exit hour.
trading.fsExplain_hoursExitReasons_read: Shows what happens at each hour: hours dominated by stops versus hours dominated by take profits. Spikes of time exits at a fixed hour come from the maximum bars rule, not the market. Compare with 5.1, where everything counts by entry.
trading.fsExplain_hoursExitStops_what: Stop losses by local exit hour, with the small hours (0h–7h) in a different shade. It is the hour the price touched the stop, regardless of when the trade opened.
trading.fsExplain_hoursExitStops_read: Spikes at session opens (London, New York) are normal: that is when volume peaks. Spikes in the small hours, with thin liquidity, suggest stops taken out by thin moves; closing earlier or not holding overnight may then be worth it. Cross with the entry → exit hour table.
trading.fsExplain_hoursExitTable_what: Per entry: the stops, the 3 local exit hours with the most stops, the average entry and exit hour of the stopped trades (circular mean on a 24 h clock), the hour with the most winning exits, and the stops within 60 minutes of entry and in the small hours (0h–7h), as % of that entry's stops.
trading.fsExplain_hoursExitTable_read: Many stops in the first hour point to a stop that is too tight or a rushed entry; many in the small hours point to positions left to overnight noise. If the average exit hour of the stops is far from the entry hour, the problem is what comes afterwards (a session that turns the price).
trading.fsExplain_hoursExitWins_what: Winning exits by local exit hour: take profit, trailing stop and break-even with positive P&L. The tooltip splits the three.
trading.fsExplain_hoursExitWins_read: Tells you when trades tend to reach their target. If gains concentrate in one session and stops in another (chart beside it), there is a favourable window; holding outside it may just give the market time to turn against you.
trading.fsExplain_hoursFilters_what: Schedule filters chosen only from the in-sample trades — the 3 worst hours by expectancy, hours with 50% or more stops, the worst day, only the 8 best hours, worst hours + worst day, the hour with most stops hit and the one before, the small hours 00h–05h, the London and New York opens and weekdays only (hours with 3 or more trades) — then run in the engine with those hours or days added to the blocked times. For each: signals blocked, trades, stops, return, max drawdown, Δ versus current and in- and out-of-sample return (split as in 3.1), with the out-of-sample Δ.
trading.fsExplain_hoursFilters_read: The deciding column is the out-of-sample Δ: a filter that improves in sample but not out of it is memorising the past. Prefer filters that improve out of sample, reduce the drawdown and do not cut half the trades. A positive total Δ is almost guaranteed, since the filter was chosen by looking at that data.
trading.fsExplain_hoursFilters_pros:
Really run in the engine, with everything it changes (capital, pauses, positions).
The in/out split shows whether the filter is real.
trading.fsExplain_hoursFilters_cons:
The out-of-sample part is a single sample and can be right by chance.
With few trades out of sample, the out-of-sample Δ is unstable.
trading.fsExplain_hoursFunding_what: The three daily funding charges (00h, 08h and 16h UTC): how often a position was open, the % and the total funding of those charges, computed as in the engine (quantity × price × rate, signed by position side). Paid shows negative, received positive. Without funding (spot or funding off), only positions are counted.
trading.fsExplain_hoursFunding_read: If one charge weighs a lot, positions opened before that hour pay it; closing earlier or entering just after avoids it. Compare with total P&L: in thin-margin strategies funding can eat the profit.
trading.fsExplain_hoursFunding_cons:
Only exists on perpetuals with funding on.
Future funding changes with the market.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapBiggest_what: The first hour of a UTC day that moved most in the period, with its sign and date.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapBiggest_read: The largest shock the daily candle open brought; if it exceeds the stop, a stop could have been jumped. Look at that date on the price chart.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapCost_what: How much those stops cost beyond exiting exactly at the stop level: the difference between the level and the exit price × the quantity, in the position's direction; the exit price already includes slippage.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapCost_read: Compare with total P&L: if it is a meaningful fraction, review the size or where the stop sits. Zero means no stop was jumped.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapCost_cons:
Only counts jumped stops.
Does not include fees.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapCrossing_what: The trades opened before a UTC midnight and closed after it, and their % of all; and of these, those crossing a Saturday, Sunday or Monday midnight (the weekend).
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapCrossing_read: A high % means the strategy lives through the daily candle and the weekend; compare these groups' P&L in the passage table. Intraday strategies should have this near zero.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapDaily_what: One bar per UTC day with the first-hour change (00h to 01h), blue up and orange down; in the footer, the largest drop and rise, the number of days and the absolute average, also for Mondays alone.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapDaily_read: Look for clusters of big bars (volatile phases) and whether Mondays move more than other days. If the Monday average is clearly larger, the weekend builds up risk.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapDays_what: The UTC days in the period with candles in the first hour (00h–01h), and how many were Mondays. Each gives one bar in the 00h UTC candle chart.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapDays_read: The sample size of crypto «gaps». Mondays count separately because they concentrate the weekend effect of traditional markets.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapMean_what: The average absolute change in the first hour of each UTC day: from the open of the 00h minute to the close of the last minute before 01h.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapMean_read: Compare with the stop: if the average move is a large fraction of the stop %, crossing UTC midnight is a risk. Also compare with the Monday average in the chart footer.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapStops_what: Stop losses where the exit minute already opened beyond the stop level: the price jumped the stop and the exit was worse than planned.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapStops_read: Few or none is normal in crypto, which trades non-stop. Many point to stops in areas of sharp moves or thin markets; see the cost in the next card and the extra stop cost in 4.3.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGapStops_cons:
1-minute candles hide jumps inside the minute.
Only counts stops with a defined level.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridPnl_what: The average P&L per trade in each day × hour cell, in the quote currency, from orange to blue, with a symmetric scale up to the 90th percentile of absolute values (above it, the end colour). The tooltip also gives total P&L; fewer than 5 trades is faded.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridPnl_read: The map closest to money: continuous blue areas with enough trades are the core of the strategy; persistent orange areas are filter candidates. The 90th percentile keeps one extreme cell from washing out the rest.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridPnl_cons:
Averages of few trades mislead.
Cells above the 90th percentile look the same even when very different.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridStops_what: The same grid with each cell's stop losses (by entry): «-» = trades but no stops, empty = no trades. Cells with fewer than 5 trades are faded.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridStops_read: The candidates to block are cells with many trades and many stops (the % is in the tooltip). An orange cell with 2 trades means nothing. Confirm the effect in 5.8 before creating blocked times.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridTrades_what: A 7 × 24 map: in each cell (weekday × local entry hour) the number of trades opened; the darker the blue, the more trades.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridTrades_read: Shows patterns the hour and day views hide, such as an hour that is only active on Mondays. It is the base for the other three maps: a cell with few trades should not weigh on their conclusions.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridWinRate_what: The win rate (trades with positive P&L) of each day × hour cell, only for cells with 3 or more trades; from orange (below 50%) to blue (above), with 50% in the middle.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridWinRate_read: Read it with the payoff: a trend strategy can make money with a 35% win rate. Look for continuous areas of the same colour, more credible than isolated cells. With 3 to 5 trades, a 0% or 100% win rate is mostly luck.
trading.fsExplain_hoursGridWinRate_cons:
Ignores the size of gains and losses.
3 trades is still very few.
trading.fsExplain_hoursMonthDay_what: The summed P&L (from daily equity) by day of the month, 1 to 31, and below the total of the first 5 and last 5 days of each month (by each month's length).
trading.fsExplain_hoursMonthDay_read: Shows whether month ends and starts, with rebalancing and expiries, matter. Days 29 to 31 occur less often, so they weigh less; look for large, consistent differences, not single bars.
trading.fsExplain_hoursMonthDay_cons:
Days 29 to 31 do not exist in every month.
Calendar effects in crypto are weak and shifting.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPassage_what: Two tables in UTC. The first splits trades by what they cross — close the same day, cross the daily candle, cross the weekend (the three separate) — and into longs, shorts and all, with P&L, stops and gapped stops. The second runs the strategy in the engine with session rules (close on Friday 20h UTC and no entries until Sunday 23h, no entries at the weekend, close everything at the NY close, no entries in the 00h UTC candle), with return, Δ, max drawdown, out-of-sample return and out-of-sample Δ.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPassage_read: If trades crossing the weekend lose, closing on Friday should improve the return; confirm it in the out-of-sample Δ. A positive Δ only in the total is coincidence; a rule that cuts the drawdown without losing return is a good trade-off.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPassage_cons:
The rules are fixed (only four).
Groups such as the weekend may have few trades.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPnl_what: The summed net P&L of the trades opened in each local hour, in the quote currency: blue bars up for gains, orange bars down for losses. Hours with fewer than 5 trades are faded (small sample).
trading.fsExplain_hoursPnl_read: Look for runs of consecutive hours with the same sign: a continuous window of losses is more credible than an isolated hour. Ignore faded bars. Confirm in 5.8 (in vs out of sample) before blocking hours.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPnl_cons:
A sum: an hour with many trades weighs more.
One big trade can flip an entire hour.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPosDuration_what: The average trade duration, in candles of the simulation's timeframe, by local entry hour.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPosDuration_read: Trades opened late in the day that last long cross the night and the daily candle (and, in futures, the 00h UTC funding). Hours with much longer durations than the rest are usually entries in a quiet market, waiting for the next session.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPosOpen_what: The average number of open positions in each local hour over the period: the time trades spent inside each hour divided by that hour's total time in the period. The small hours (0h–7h) are in another colour.
trading.fsExplain_hoursPosOpen_read: The exposure profile through the day: 0.5 in an hour means a position was open during half of those hours. High exposure in the small hours means risk when nobody is watching and thinner liquidity.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSampleBest_what: The mirror: the 6 hours with the best in-sample expectancy (3 or more trades) and what they did out of sample, with the win rate instead of the stop %.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSampleBest_read: If the best hours stay positive out of sample, the strategy has a real window and an «Only the 8 best hours» schedule may be worth it (see the filter table above). If they turn negative, the edge is not in the hour.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSampleBest_pros:
Shows whether the hourly edge persists.
Complements the worst hours.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSampleBest_cons:
Small sample per hour.
The past's best hours tend to regress to the mean.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSampleWorst_what: The 6 local entry hours with the worst expectancy (average P&L) in the in-sample part, only with 3 or more trades, and what they did out of sample: trades, expectancy and stop % in each part, and whether the expectancy kept its sign.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSampleWorst_read: «Keeps its sign» on almost all means the bad hours persist and a filter makes sense. If most flip sign, the worst hours were chance and blocking them will not help.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSampleWorst_pros:
A direct persistence test, hour by hour.
Simple to read.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSampleWorst_cons:
Few trades per hour in each part.
The sign may hold by chance.
trading.fsExplain_hoursSessionMoments_what: For three moments — the daily candle close (00h UTC) and the New York open (9:30) and close (16:00) in New York time, weekdays only — how often a position was open, the % of occurrences, the trades that crossed them and their P&L. The local time column shows when the moment falls in the simulation's time zone (it shifts with daylight saving).
trading.fsExplain_hoursSessionMoments_read: A high % at the NY open means the strategy is usually exposed to the moment of highest volume and volatility. If trades crossing a moment lose, test closing before it (5.9, close at the NY close).
trading.fsExplain_hoursStopsChart_what: Per entry hour, the trades that closed at the stop loss (whenever that was), with the hour's stop % above each bar. The tooltip gives trades, stops and the %.
trading.fsExplain_hoursStopsChart_read: Look for bars with a % above the strategy's average and many trades: those are the hours where entering is costly. A high % in an hour with 2 or 3 trades means nothing. Compare with the P&L next to it and with 5.2, where the same stops count by exit hour.
trading.fsExplain_hoursStopsEntry_what: The entry hour with the most trades closed at the stop loss, counted by the hour they opened, whenever they closed. Only the stop loss counts (not trailing or break-even); the detail gives that hour's stops and trades.
trading.fsExplain_hoursStopsEntry_read: Compare the stops with the hour's trades: 8 stops out of 10 trades is a problem, 8 out of 40 may be normal. If it is also the busiest hour, it is just volume; what matters is the stop %, in the 5.1 table and the 5.4 map.
trading.fsExplain_hoursStopsExit_what: The local hour in which the most stop losses were hit: the same stops as the previous card, but counted by the hour the trade closed.
trading.fsExplain_hoursStopsExit_read: If it differs from the entry hour with the most stops, the problem is what the market does afterwards: for example, the New York open sweeping stops of morning entries. See 5.2 for the full profile and the entry → exit hour table.
trading.fsExplain_hoursTable_what: One row per local entry hour (all 24): the session (Asia 0–7h, Europe 8–13h, overlap 14–16h, US 17–21h, night 22–23h, in local hours), trades and % of total, longs/shorts, win rate, stops and %, P&L, expectancy (average P&L per trade), average R (only trades with a stop), average bars held and the entry that opened most.
trading.fsExplain_hoursTable_read: Expectancy and average R compare hours with different trade counts, unlike summed P&L. An hour with negative average R and a high stop %, with enough trades, is a filter candidate. Check whether the good hours cluster in one session.
trading.fsExplain_hoursWeeks_what: The net P&L of each week (Monday to Sunday, from daily equity), blue or orange, with the number of stops above each week (up to 80 weeks; beyond that, only in the tooltip) and the positive weeks in the footer.
trading.fsExplain_hoursWeeks_read: Shows week-by-week regularity and the good and bad phases. Many positive weeks without huge negative ones signal a stable curve; long runs of orange weeks show regimes where the strategy does not work (see 3.6).
