trading.fsExplain_hoursWork_what: In the simulation's local time: working hours (Monday to Friday, 9h–18h), evening and night (Mon–Fri 18h–24h), the small hours (0h–7h, every day), the weekend and each UTC offset (winter and summer time). For each: the hours of that kind in the period, trades (by entry), trades per 100 hours, win rate, P&L and expectancy. Below, the P&L inside versus outside working hours.
trading.fsExplain_hoursWork_read: «Trades / 100 h» normalises by the size of each period. If the strategy wins mostly outside working hours, it must run on its own with reliable stops; if it wins during working hours, it can be supervised. Winter versus summer differences point to dependence on the exchanges, which shift their hours.
trading.fsExplain_hoursWorld_what: Per world session in fixed UTC hours (Sydney 22h–07h, Tokyo 00h–09h, London 08h–17h, New York 13h–22h, and the overlaps London + NY, Sydney + Tokyo and Sydney only): the trades opened in it by UTC entry hour, win rate, stops, P&L, expectancy and volatility, the average range (high − low over open) of the 1-hour candles in those hours. A trade in an overlap counts in both sessions.
trading.fsExplain_hoursWorld_read: Look for the session with the best expectancy and whether it matches high volatility (breakout strategies) or low (mean reversion). The London and New York overlap usually has the most volume and movement.
trading.fsExplain_hoursWorld_cons:
Fixed hours, without the exchanges' daylight saving.
Sessions overlap, so the rows do not add up to the total.
trading.fsExplain_hoursWorst_what: The entry hour with the smallest summed net P&L, with the % of the trades opened in it that closed at the stop loss.
trading.fsExplain_hoursWorst_read: An hour with negative P&L and many stops is the most obvious candidate to block, but first check in 5.8 whether the filter holds out of sample. A slightly negative P&L on few trades is probably noise.
trading.fsExplain_proofCostStress_what: The strategy run again in the engine with higher costs: commission (entry and exit) at ×2 and ×3, slippage plus 0.05 and plus 0.1 percentage points, and commission ×2 with +0.05 slippage. For each: commissions paid, return, the gap in percentage points to the current one, max drawdown (on the index), profit factor and out-of-sample return. Below, the commission at which return reaches zero, interpolated between ×1, ×2 and ×3.
trading.fsExplain_proofCostStress_read: A healthy strategy keeps winning with commission at ×2 (that is what the verdict requires). If return collapses with +0.05% slippage, it lives on short trades with thin margins and in practice, with real spreads and fills, may not make money. The further the break-even point is from ×1, the more headroom there is. Compare with the costs in 1.1 (their share of gross profit).
trading.fsExplain_proofCostStress_pros:
Tests one of the most common reasons good backtests fail live.
Full engine run: costs also change later position sizes and capital.
trading.fsExplain_proofCostStress_cons:
Multipliers are fixed; it does not model spreads widening under stress.
Slippage only applies to market orders, stops, breakouts and forced exits; limit orders do not pay it.
The break-even point is a linear interpolation up to ×3; beyond that it reads «not reached».
trading.fsExplain_proofMarkets_what: The same strategy, with the same period, timeframe, parameters and warm-up, run on other markets of the same type (spot with spot, futures with futures; up to 10 at a time). Each market becomes a new simulation linked to this one, with its full report; only the quantity and notional minimums switch to the new market's. The table gathers the whole family: result, buy & hold, trades, win rate, max drawdown and verdict for each. Clicking a row opens it.
trading.fsExplain_proofMarkets_read: A strategy built on a real idea usually wins, or at least does not lose much, on similar markets (for instance, other large cryptocurrencies). If it only wins on this market, it is fitted to it. Always compare with each market's buy & hold and with the verdict: several «robust» are worth more than one isolated high return.
trading.fsExplain_proofMarkets_pros:
One of the strongest tests against overfitting: brand-new data with the same rules.
Each market has the full report, with the same proofs.
The simulations stay linked and show up here again.
trading.fsExplain_proofMarkets_cons:
Highly correlated markets (BTC and ETH) are not independent data; winning on all may be the same market repeated.
Parameters in % (stop, take) may not make sense on an asset with different volatility.
Each market is a full simulation: it takes time and needs the candles downloaded.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcDrawdown_what: The largest peak-to-trough drop that only 5% of the 1000 paths exceed (95th percentile of each path's max drawdown), with the median below. The drop is measured on each path's capital, without deposits.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcDrawdown_read: This is the drawdown worth preparing for, not the backtest's. If it is bigger than you could stomach (financially or mentally), position size is too large. Compare with the real drawdown next to it and with the histogram below.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcDrawdown_pros:
Gives a more honest worst case than the max drawdown of a single backtest.
Useful for sizing risk and capital before trading.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcDrawdown_cons:
The real worst case can be bigger: resampling does not create crises the period did not have.
With 10-day blocks, very long losing streaks may be underestimated.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcDrops_what: The histogram of the max drawdown of each of the 1000 paths, in 30 bars from 0% to the largest drop seen; the bar where the real drawdown falls is in another colour. Below, the % of paths that fall 10, 20, 30 and 50% or more.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcDrops_read: A distribution packed to the left is a good sign: big drops are rare. A long right tail means some paths have far bigger drops than the real one. If the real bar sits on the left, the backtest shows optimistic risk (compare with the «Real drawdown» card).
trading.fsExplain_proofMcFan_what: Cumulative return over time: the dashed line is the median of the 1000 paths, the dark band runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile and the light one from the 5th to the 95th; the solid line is the real path. Percentiles are computed on up to 200 days spread across the period.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcFan_read: The real line inside the 25–75 band is a typical result. If it spends a long time hugging the top of the 5–95 band, the backtest had a favourable day order. A band that opens wide downwards shows that, with the same strategy, the path could have been much worse; a narrow rising band signals consistent profit.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcFan_cons:
Bands are per-day percentiles, not real paths: no path follows the median from start to finish.
Only reuses the period's days (drawn in blocks, with replacement): the fan does not include markets that never happened.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcLoss_what: The % of the 1000 Monte Carlo paths that end with capital below the start. Each path is built from the daily returns of the performance index (no deposits) drawn in blocks of 10 consecutive days (with replacement), up to the same number of days as the backtest; the seed is fixed, so the result is repeatable.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcLoss_read: Below 20% is good (the verdict counts the test as passed); 20% to 40% is undecided; above 40% fails. Read it as the probability that the same strategy, with the same days in another order, would have ended at a loss. Cross it with the median return and the real result's percentile next to it.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcLoss_pros:
Sums up in one number how much the profit depends on the order the days fell in.
10-day blocks keep good and bad phases together, more realistic than drawing single days.
Feeds straight into the verdict.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcLoss_cons:
Only reuses days that already happened: it does not invent crises or markets the period did not have.
Assumes blocks are interchangeable; dependence between phases longer than 10 days is lost.
In a short period there are few distinct blocks and the paths look too alike.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcReal_what: The backtest return on the performance index (no deposits) and the percentile it reaches among the 1000 Monte Carlo paths: the % of paths that ended with a return equal to or below the real one.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcReal_read: Around 50 is expected: the backtest is a typical path. Close to 100 means the real day order was one of the most favourable, and the future should sit closer to the median. Close to 0 is the opposite: the backtest landed on a bad order and the strategy may be worth more than it looks.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcReal_cons:
A high percentile does not prove overfitting; a middle one does not prove robustness either.
Inherits the limits of block resampling (only the days that existed).
trading.fsExplain_proofMcRealDrawdown_what: The backtest's max drawdown on the performance index (no deposits) and the percentile it reaches among the 1000 paths: the % of paths whose max drawdown is equal to or smaller than the real one.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcRealDrawdown_read: A low percentile means the real drawdown was among the smallest possible: the backtest shows optimistic risk and the next drawdown is likely bigger. Around 50 is typical; high means the backtest already caught one of the worst orders.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcRealDrawdown_cons:
Limited to the period's days, like the rest of the Monte Carlo.
A single big drop in the period weighs heavily on the percentile.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcReturn_what: The final return of the middle path (50th percentile) of the 1000 drawn paths, with the 5th and 95th percentiles below: 90% of paths end between those two values. It is the return on the performance index, without deposits.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcReturn_read: A positive median and a positive P5 say the profit does not depend on the luck of the day order. A very negative P5 with a good median means the strategy can end badly even if it is good on average. Compare with the real return: if the real one is well above the median, the backtest caught a favourable order.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcReturn_cons:
Every path uses the same days: the range is about order, not about the future.
Blocks are drawn with replacement: some stretches repeat and others are left out, and one exceptional day weighs heavily on the paths it enters.
Does not account for costs or markets different from the period's.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcRuin_what: The % of the 1000 paths that at some point fall 50% or more from a previous peak (not just at the end). The other levels (10, 20 and 30%) are below the max drawdown histogram.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcRuin_read: Ideally 0% or close. Anything above a few % says losing half the account is a plausible scenario with this strategy and position size. Smaller size lowers this number; if it does not, the problem is losing streaks.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcRuin_pros:
Puts the risk of ruin into an easy-to-share number.
Counts drops along the way, which is where people quit or get liquidated.
trading.fsExplain_proofMcRuin_cons:
50% is a fixed level; each person's or account's ruin may differ (in a prop firm it is much lower).
Does not see crises outside the period; 0% does not mean impossible.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropDaysToPass_what: The median number of days to reach the target, only for the weekly challenges that passed. Below, the days with entries over the whole period and the minimum required by the rules.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropDaysToPass_read: Well below the deadline is good: there is room for a bad start. Close to the deadline means those that pass do so narrowly. If the period's trading days are close to the minimum, the strategy trades little and may not meet that rule in a short challenge.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropDrawdown_what: The largest distance from peak capital over the period, with positions at each minute's worst price and no deposits. Below, the max loss limit. Under the static rule the limit counts from initial capital; under the trailing rule it counts from the highest point reached, by a fixed amount equal to the % of initial capital.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropDrawdown_read: If it passes the limit it turns orange: the account would have been closed. Under the static rule, a big drop after a good profit may not break the rule (the limit sits down at the initial capital); under trailing it does, which makes it tougher. Compare with the Monte Carlo drawdown (3.2): the next one may be bigger.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropFailed_what: How many of the weekly challenges broke a rule before the target and, below, how many by daily loss, how many by max loss, and how many ran out of time without passing or failing (undecided).
trading.fsExplain_proofPropFailed_read: It turns orange when there are more fails than passes. The rule that fails most says what to fix: many daily-loss fails call for less risk per day or a daily trade limit; many max-loss fails call for smaller positions. Many undecided mean the strategy is too slow for the deadline or target.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropPassRate_what: A challenge of the rules' length starting on every Monday of the period (local midnight), each with capital reset at the start. The % that reach the target, with the minimum days, before breaking a rule and within the deadline. It is an approximation: the trades are the simulation's, scaled to the reset capital.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropPassRate_read: Above 50% turns blue: more than half the attempts would pass. It is far more representative than the whole period, because it tests many starting points. Below 30%, paying for several challenges until one passes tends to cost more than it earns.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropPassRate_pros:
Answers the practical question: how many attempts until a pass?
Tests many different starts, not just the first day.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropPassRate_cons:
Windows overlap and share trades: they are not independent attempts.
The scaling approximation is only exact with size as a % of capital; with fixed amounts it drifts.
Does not include the entry fee or each firm's extra rules.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropWhole_what: The whole period treated as a single prop firm challenge, from the start and with no deadline. Rules are checked minute by minute on realised capital (no deposits) plus the floating P&L of open positions at each minute's worst price (the low for a long, the high for a short). It passes if realised capital reaches the target with the minimum trading days before the daily loss or max loss is broken; below, when and why.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropWhole_read: «Passed» early is the best sign. «Failed» says which rule broke first and on what day: often it is the daily loss, from one bad day early on. «Undecided» means it never reached the target nor broke a rule. Read it with the % of challenges that pass, which is more representative.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropWhole_cons:
A single starting point; starting a week later may give a different result.
Each prop firm's real rules have details (day close, consistency, news) that are not modelled here.
No deadline, unlike a real challenge.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropWindows_what: A strip with one square per Monday on which a challenge of the rules' length starts, in time order, coloured by outcome: passed, failed or undecided. On hover: the date, outcome, days taken and the rule broken.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropWindows_read: Check whether failures are spread out or clustered. Clustered in one period means the strategy suffers in one type of market (compare with the 3.6 regimes); spread out, that risk per day is too high in general. A strip that gets worse towards the end is a bad sign, as in 3.1.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropWorstDay_what: The largest drop within a day, in the simulation's local time, measured from the capital at the start of that day (positions at the close) to the day's lowest point, with open positions at each minute's worst price. Below, the daily loss limit from the rules.
trading.fsExplain_proofPropWorstDay_read: If it is beyond (more negative than) the limit, the strategy breaks the daily rule at least once and turns orange. Leave headroom: a worst day at half the limit leaves room for a day worse than the backtest's. If it is close to the limit, smaller positions are the most direct fix.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeChart_what: The annualised return of the strategy and of buy & hold on the days of each trend: up (the daily close above the 200-day average, which is rising over 20 days), down (below and falling) and sideways (the rest). Each day takes the previous day's regime, to avoid looking ahead. It is only annualised with 30 or more days in a regime.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeChart_read: Ideally the strategy wins in at least two trends (as the verdict requires); if it only wins in the uptrend, it is disguised buy & hold and fails the test. Making less than buy & hold in the uptrend and losing less in the downtrend is the typical profile of a capital-protecting strategy. Missing bars mean the period did not have that regime.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeGrid_what: Crossing the three trends with the two volatility levels: each of the 6 cells shows the strategy's annualised return on the days of that combination (or the compounded one, with fewer than 30 days), the days and the trades. Colour goes from orange (losing) to blue (winning), up to the largest absolute value; «—» means there were no days.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeGrid_read: A robust strategy has several blue cells, not just one. A single strong cell (say, uptrend with high volatility) says profit depends on a very specific market. Always check the cell's days: deep blue over 15 days barely counts.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeGrid_cons:
Six cells split the days and trades; many end up with small samples.
Colour is the annualised return, which exaggerates cells with few days.
Filtering on the good cell after seeing it is overfitting; test the filter and confirm out of sample.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeTable_what: By trend regime (up, sideways, down) and volatility regime (high or low: 30-day annualised volatility above or below the period's median), using the previous day's regime: days and % of the period, the strategy's compounded and annualised return (on the index, no deposits), annualised buy & hold, and the trades of those days (by entry day) with win rate, P&L and expectancy. «No data» are the days before an average or volatility exists.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeTable_read: Look for positive expectancy in several regimes. A trend strategy usually wins in high volatility and suffers sideways; a mean-reversion one, the opposite. If nearly all P&L comes from a regime that covered little of the period, the result depends on that regime returning. Cross with 3.1: a different regime in and out of sample explains a lot of degradation.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeTable_pros:
Shows which market the strategy wins in and where it loses.
Separates the return of the days (index) from the result of the trades opened on them.
trading.fsExplain_proofRegimeTable_cons:
Regimes are relative to the period (the volatility median changes between simulations).
A trade counts in the regime of its entry day, even if it spans several regimes.
Regimes with few days or trades give unreliable numbers.
trading.fsExplain_proofSampleEquity_what: The capital of each day, as in the 1.2 curve (with deposits), with a dashed line on the day the period is split and the out-of-sample part shaded. The split day is exactly the one in the 3.1 table. Underneath: the first day, the split day and the last day.
trading.fsExplain_proofSampleEquity_read: Look for a curve that keeps the same slope and kind of swings after the line. A clean rise up to the line and a flat or falling curve afterwards is the typical shape of a strategy fitted to the past. A drop right after the split that later recovers may just be a bad patch: check with the Monte Carlo (3.2) and walk-forward (3.3).
trading.fsExplain_proofSampleEquity_cons:
Includes deposits, so a rise may be new money rather than profit; the 3.1 table uses the index without deposits.
No visible axes: it is for the shape, not for reading values (hover to see them).
A single split; a different market regime on each side weighs heavily on how it looks.
trading.fsExplain_proofSampleSplit_what: The table splits the period in two: in-sample (the beginning) and out-of-sample (the end, the % set in «Out of sample» under Validation; without it, the last 30%, as in the score). The split falls at UTC midnight of that day, the same instant used by the score, the per-entry tables and the variants. Trades count by entry time; annualised return, Sharpe and max drawdown come from the performance index (no deposits) on each part's days, and buy & hold from the price. «Degradation» is (out − in) ÷ |in| in %.
trading.fsExplain_proofSampleSplit_read: A positive degradation is always better outside (drawdown is negative so it reads the same way). The red flag is a profit, profit factor or R expectancy that turns from positive to negative outside: most likely the strategy was tuned to history. A 20–40% drop is normal; above 50% deserves suspicion. Compare with the buy & hold of each part (a worse market outside explains part of the drop) and with the walk-forward (3.3), which repeats the test over 6 windows.
trading.fsExplain_proofSampleSplit_pros:
The most direct test against overfitting: it shows what the strategy does on data that did not shape the choices.
Puts the metrics that matter side by side, with the same split across the whole report.
The buy & hold of each part helps separate the strategy from the market.
trading.fsExplain_proofSampleSplit_cons:
Only valid if the parameters were chosen without looking at the outside part; once you look and adjust, it is no longer out-of-sample.
A single split: the result depends on where it falls and on the market regime on each side.
With few trades outside, percentages swing a lot (the degradation of a win rate over 8 trades says almost nothing).
Degradation in % misleads when the in-sample value is close to zero.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensGrid_what: A 5 × 5 map of the two parameters whose steps moved the return most (the largest spread in the table), changed together from ×0.8 to ×1.2; the current one is in the centre. Each cell is an engine run and shows the return; colour goes from orange (losing) to blue (winning) on a symmetric scale. On hover: the out-of-sample return, drawdown and trades.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensGrid_read: A wide patch of the same colour around the centre is robust: small parameter errors do not break the strategy. A blue centre surrounded by orange is an isolated peak, a sign of overfitting. If the strongest blue is in a corner, the current parameters are not the best and the good zone may extend past the map.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensGrid_pros:
Shows the interaction between the two most sensitive parameters, which the table cannot.
Reads at a glance: shape and colour.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensGrid_cons:
Only two parameters; the rest stay fixed.
Covers only ±20%: the good zone may extend beyond the edges.
Only exists with two or more parameters, and each map costs 24 runs.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensOut_what: The % of the same 3.4 variants that win in the out-of-sample part, split on the same day as 3.1. The outside return is that of the performance index (no deposits) from the split day.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensOut_read: Above 50% is a good sign: the neighbours of the chosen parameters also work on new data. If the whole-period % is high but the outside one is low, the in-sample period is carrying every variant's result. Compare with 3.1.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensOut_cons:
Out-of-sample has fewer days and trades, so the % swings more.
Only meaningful if the parameters were not tuned looking at the outside part.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensParams_what: How many strategy parameters were changed, and the steps for each (×0.8, ×0.9, ×1.1, ×1.2). Included: each average's period (by indicator, in every condition using it), the last N bars, each entry's stop, take, trailing and break-even, setup bars and the numbers of stop adjustments and scale-ins. Only version 3 strategies have parameters.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensParams_read: More parameters means more freedom to fit the past: a strategy with many needs more trades to be credible. Each parameter costs 4 extra runs in the report. If an expected parameter is missing, it was not set (for instance, no trailing means no trailing to change).
trading.fsExplain_proofSensPositive_what: The % of variants that end in profit over the whole period. Each variant is the strategy run again in the engine with a single parameter changed to ×0.8, ×0.9, ×1.1 or ×1.2 (each average's period, the last N bars, stop, take, trailing, break-even, setup bars and the numbers of stop adjustments and scale-ins).
trading.fsExplain_proofSensPositive_read: 80% or more is good (the verdict passes the test); below 50% fails. A robust strategy keeps winning when parameters move a little; if only the exact values win, they were picked at the peak of history. The table below shows which parameter breaks it.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensPositive_pros:
Measures directly how much the result depends on the chosen numbers.
Uses the whole strategy, run in the engine, not an approximation.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensPositive_cons:
Changes one parameter at a time: combinations only in the map of the two that move it most.
Longer periods may miss the first signals, because the downloaded warm-up is the simulation's.
Counts only the sign of the return: a variant making 0.1% counts like one making 50%.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensRank_what: The percentile of the strategy as it is among all the 3.4 variants: the % of variants with a return equal to or lower than the current one.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensRank_read: A middle or high but not extreme value is ideal: the parameters sit in a good zone. Close to 100 (above 90 it turns orange) means the current one beats almost every neighbour: an isolated peak, the typical sign of parameters picked at the historical maximum. A low value says some neighbouring parameters are better (see which in the table).
trading.fsExplain_proofSensRank_cons:
A high percentile also happens when the strategy is genuinely well tuned in a wide zone; check the map.
Compares against few variants (4 per parameter).
trading.fsExplain_proofSensTable_what: One row per parameter, with the strategy's return at each step (×0.8, ×0.9, current, ×1.1, ×1.2) and, below, the value used and the out-of-sample return. Colour is the return; the current cell is outlined. «Spread» is the gap, in percentage points, between the best and worst step (including the current one); «Winning», the % of the 4 steps with a positive return.
trading.fsExplain_proofSensTable_read: Rows of uniform colour with a low spread are stable parameters. A row that flips from blue to orange next to the current cell is the fragile parameter: it is where the strategy can fail. Out-of-sample returns that change sign between neighbouring steps confirm that parameter is fitting noise.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfBeat_what: How many of the 5 windows (from the 2nd on) the variant chosen by the previous window returned more than the strategy as it is, in the same window.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfBeat_read: More than half means re-optimising helps. Few or none means the current parameters are already as good as those picked from the recent best, and changing parameters now and then only adds noise. Read it with the «Walk-forward» card (the total).
trading.fsExplain_proofWfBeat_pros:
Answers a practical question: is re-optimising worth it?
Compares within the same window, so the market is the same for both.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfBeat_cons:
A window won by a hair counts as much as one won by a mile.
If the chosen variant is the current one, it ties and does not count as a win.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChain_what: The compounded return of the walk-forward chain: from the 2nd to the 6th window, each uses the parameter variant (from the 3.4 runs, plus the current one) that had the best return in the previous window, without seeing the future. Below, the fixed strategy over the same 5 windows, for comparison.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChain_read: If the chain is close to or above the fixed one, periodic re-optimisation does not hurt and may help. If it is well below, yesterday's best parameter does not tell tomorrow's: prefer stable values (a wide zone in 3.4) over re-optimising. A negative chain with a positive fixed result warns that fine-tuning is noise.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChain_pros:
Simulates the real process of re-optimising without looking ahead.
Uses the same variants as 3.4, so the two sections talk to each other.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChain_cons:
Only picks among one-parameter variants (×0.8 to ×1.2), not a full optimisation.
Picks on return alone, ignoring risk and trade count.
Older strategies (before version 3) have no variants, so the chain repeats the current one.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChart_what: Bars of the return of each of the 6 windows: the strategy as it is, the variant chosen by the previous window (from the 2nd) and buy & hold in the same window. Returns are on the performance index (no deposits) and, for buy & hold, on the price.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChart_read: Look for strategy bars that are positive in most windows, especially in windows where buy & hold falls. If the walk-forward bar is consistently below the strategy's, re-optimising does not pay. One window far above the rest explains a large part of the profit on its own.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChosen_what: How many of the 5 windows (from the 2nd on) the variant chosen by the previous window ended with a positive return in the next one.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChosen_read: Most winning says parameters chosen from past information keep working in the near future. Few winning, especially if the fixed strategy wins more often, means picking the recent best catches noise.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfChosen_cons:
Only 5 windows: a difference of one is large in %.
Does not say how much it won or lost, only the sign.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfPositive_what: The period is split into 6 windows with the same number of days. The card counts how many the strategy, as it is, ended with a positive return (on the performance index, no deposits) and, below, how many it beat buy & hold in the same window.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfPositive_read: 4 or more positive windows out of 6 is good (the verdict passes the test at 4; at 2 or fewer it fails). Profit concentrated in one or two windows means the result comes from one market phase. Beating buy & hold in most windows is tougher and more telling on an asset that rose a lot.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfPositive_cons:
6 windows is a small sample; one window more or less changes the reading a lot.
Windows of equal length can have very different trade counts.
Does not test the parameters: it is the same strategy in every window.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfTable_what: One row per window, with dates: the return and drawdown of the strategy as it is, buy & hold, trades (by entry), the variant chosen by the previous window and its return here, and this window's best variant and its return. This window's best is only for comparison: it was picked looking back.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfTable_read: Compare the «Its return» column with the strategy's «Return»: that is the gain or loss from re-optimising. If this window's best is almost always another variant and much better, the result depends heavily on parameters and the optimum shifts from window to window. If the same variant keeps being chosen, it is a parameter worth considering.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfWorst_what: The return of the worst of the 6 windows for the strategy as it is, on the performance index (no deposits). Each window is about one sixth of the period.
trading.fsExplain_proofWfWorst_read: Gives an idea of the worst multi-month stretch to expect. A slightly negative worst window is normal; a very negative one says there are phases where the strategy loses a lot, and the table below shows whether it matches a falling market (that window's buy & hold).
trading.fsExplain_setupArming_what: For each entry with a setup: the rule in words and what happened to it, counted by the engine. Armed (the setup was met with the entry unarmed), renewed (met again while armed and the candle count restarted), expired (the candles ran out without a signal), cancelled (the cancel conditions were met first), fired (the entry's conditions were met while armed, with the % of times it armed), the average candles to the signal and the signals and trades that came from it.
trading.fsExplain_setupArming_read: The «fired» % says how many setups actually get used. A very low % with many «expired» suggests the candle window is short or the entry condition is rare; many «renewed» mean the setup is met almost all the time and filters little. Candles to signal help choose the window: if the signal almost always comes on the first or second candle, a longer window adds little. The signals flow into the funnel above.
trading.fsExplain_setupByEntry_what: For each entry: the signals (the same as in the funnel), closed trades, the % of signals that became a trade, win rate, net P&L (after fees and funding) and expectancy in R. Each trade's R is its P&L over what it would lose at its stop (quantity × entry price × distance to the stop); expectancy is the mean of those R. Without a stop there is no R.
trading.fsExplain_setupByEntry_read: Expectancy above 0R makes money on average; above 0.2–0.3R per trade is already interesting, as long as there are enough trades (a few dozen). A low % of signals executed means the rules or level orders let little through: see the funnel above and the order variants (2.3). Compare with 4.1, which shows the same entry in more detail and in vs out of sample.
trading.fsExplain_setupByEntry_cons:
With few trades per entry, win rate and expectancy vary a lot by chance.
P&L depends on order and on capital at the time; entries that depend on each other cannot be judged in isolation.
Without a stop there is no R, and the comparison is left to P&L.
trading.fsExplain_setupContext_what: Each «only enter if» condition of each entry, checked at signal time against the account state (last trade, loss or win streaks, open positions, trades today, day P&L, drawdown). It shows the rule in words, the signals it stopped (each signal counts at the first condition that failed) and the % of the entry's signals, and the strategy re-run in the engine without that condition: trades, return and max DD without it, and «Adds», the current return minus the return without the rule.
trading.fsExplain_setupContext_read: A positive «Adds» means the rule helped; negative means the strategy would earn more without it. Compare max DD too: a rule that yields little but cuts the drawdown well may be worth it. A rule that stops almost every signal, or none, deserves a review. Conditions that only change with closed trades (for example a loss streak) can stop the entry for good.
trading.fsExplain_setupContext_pros:
Measures each rule's value with a real run without it, not an estimate.
Shows the effect on risk (max DD), not only on return.
Spots rules that no longer do anything.
trading.fsExplain_setupContext_cons:
Removes one rule at a time: it does not show interactions between rules.
A positive «Adds» in the past may just be overfitting; confirm with 3.1 and 3.4.
Each signal counts at the first failing condition, so later ones may seem to stop fewer than they do.
trading.fsExplain_setupData_what: The quality of the candles the run used, computed by the simulator at the end. Simulated candles (from start to end of the period) and warm-up candles (before the start, for the indicators); candles missing in the timeframe and minutes missing in the period; opening gaps (open more than 0.2% away from the previous candle's close); the average range and the largest candle ((high − low) ÷ open); the start and end prices; and the asset's annualised volatility on daily UTC closes (√365).
trading.fsExplain_setupData_read: Missing candles or minutes should be zero or close to it: on Coinbase minutes without trades have no candle, so some missing ones are normal in less liquid markets, but many make stops and level entries less reliable. Many opening gaps in a market that trades 24 h point to holes in the data. Volatility and the start and end prices give context: a long strategy on an asset that went up tenfold has an easy life (compare with buy & hold in 1.1).
trading.fsExplain_setupEntries_what: Each strategy entry on one row, following the form's four steps: enters when (the conditions, the setup and the «only enter if» rules), enters at (market or a level, with the order's candles), with how much (size and leverage) and exits (stop, take profit, trailing, break-even, partial exits, scale-ins, stop adjustments, time exit and conditional exits), plus the schedule. It is read from the saved strategy, with the same names the form uses.
trading.fsExplain_setupEntries_read: Read it as a sentence: «buy when X, at market, risking 1%, exit at a 2% stop or a 4% take». Check that each entry does what was intended, especially the direction and the exits. Whichever exit happens first wins, so many exits on one entry make it hard to see which one decides; 4.2 shows how many trades ended in each.
trading.fsExplain_setupExecution_what: The strategy re-run in the engine with each execution price for market orders: the candle open (default), the previous candle's close (the signal candle) and the first minute's average price ((open + high + low + close) ÷ 4 of that minute). The current one comes first. For each: trades, win rate, profit factor, return, max DD on the performance index (as in the Summary) and the return Δ in p.p. against the current one.
trading.fsExplain_setupExecution_read: It is a sensitivity test on the entry price. Small differences (a few p.p.) say the strategy does not depend on getting the exact price. If the previous candle's close earns much more than the open, be suspicious: in practice one cannot enter at the close of a candle that is only known once it has closed. If the first-minute average ruins the result, the edge lives in seconds and is hard to capture for real.
trading.fsExplain_setupExecution_cons:
Only tests three prices; it does not simulate longer delays or the order book.
Does not change level orders, only market ones.
The previous candle's close is optimistic and can inflate results in mean-reversion strategies.
trading.fsExplain_setupFunnel_what: Each signal's path to a trade, counted by the engine over the whole period. A signal is a candle on which an entry's conditions were met (with multi-candle orders, each active candle counts). Each signal counts only once, at the first reason that stopped it: schedule, pause after an exit, pyramid or pending order, maximum positions, opposite signal, daily limit, «do not trade if», «only enter if» or no capital. Then come the level orders placed and dropped, those rejected by the broker minimum, stops on the wrong side and the trades (all and winning).
trading.fsExplain_setupFunnel_read: Bars are scaled to the signals (simulated candles have their own scale). A block that eats most of the signals shows which rule actually runs the strategy: this may be intended or a sign the rule is badly tuned. Many minimum rejections mean capital or size is too small. Few signals compared with candles mean rare conditions and therefore few trades to draw conclusions from (see significance in the 1.1 score).
trading.fsExplain_setupGeneral_what: The general settings this simulation ran with, read from the saved strategy: market and type (spot or futures), timeframe, period, time zone, warm-up, initial capital, deposits, leverage and funding (futures only), entry and exit fees with slippage, execution price, the out-of-sample share and the prop firm challenge. Options that were switched off are shown as off.
trading.fsExplain_setupGeneral_read: Use it to confirm the simulation tested what was intended before reading the results. Check above all the fees and slippage (they should match or be worse than the broker's real ones), the period (it should cover rising, falling and sideways markets) and whether there is an out-of-sample share, which drives 3.1 and part of the score. The time zone affects everything time-based (screen 5) and the schedule rules.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdCancelled_what: Level orders that dropped before their validity ran out because the entry condition stopped being met. It only happens on entries with «If the condition fails» set to cancel and orders of more than one candle.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdCancelled_read: Many cancellations mean the signal is unstable: the condition switches on and off from candle to candle. That can protect against late entries, or cut trades that would have made money. The order variants (cancel or not without the condition) show which of the two options earns more in this strategy.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdExpired_what: Level orders that dropped without entering: price did not reach the level while the order was valid, or it did and the position could no longer open (for example maximum positions or capital). The detail gives the validity in candles when every entry uses the same number.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdExpired_read: Expired plus filled and cancelled make up the orders placed. Many expired orders suggest a level too far away or a short validity. To know whether those missed orders were good opportunities, see the order variants: if the market version or the one with twice the candles earns more, the expired orders are costing money.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdFilled_what: The % of level orders whose price reached the level within their validity and opened the position, with the number filled out of those placed. The engine searches for the touch minute by minute, on 1-minute candles.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdFilled_read: A high rate (above 70–80%) means the level is close to price and the order almost acts as a market entry at a better price. A low rate means many opportunities are lost: that may be good (only entering at the best prices) or bad (missing strong moves that never pull back). The order variants below show what would happen with another validity or at market.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdFilled_cons:
Assumes a fill whenever price touches the level; in reality, touching does not guarantee a limit order fills.
Does not say whether the filled orders were the good or the bad ones (see order types).
With few orders, the % is unreliable.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdPlaced_what: The number of orders the level entries placed over the period: one per signal that passed every rule and, instead of entering at market, left an order at a price (fixed or tracking) valid for the order's candles. Market entries do not count here.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdPlaced_read: It is the base for the other cards: filled, expired and cancelled are parts of this number. Compare with the funnel's signals (2.2) to see how many became an order. If it is zero, every entry is at market and the rest of this section says little.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdSaved_what: An estimate of the slippage limit orders did not pay: the simulation's slippage (slippagePct) applied to the entry value of each trade opened by a limit order. It is what those entries would have cost extra at market. Stop (breakout) orders pay slippage and are not included.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdSaved_read: Compare with total profit and with the costs in 1.1: if saved slippage is a large share of the profit, much of the strategy's edge comes from the entry price and is sensitive to real execution. With slippage set to 0, this card is always 0.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdSaved_cons:
It is an estimate: it ignores that limit orders miss some opportunities (see expired).
Depends entirely on the configured slippage, which may not be the real one.
Ignores maker and taker fees, which differ on some exchanges.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdWait_what: The average number of candles between the signal and the minute the level order was filled, only for orders that became a trade. 0 means it filled on the signal candle itself.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrdWait_read: A wait close to 0 means price usually touches the level right away; a wait close to the validity means many orders fill at the last moment and a shorter validity would miss them. The longer the wait, the more the market may have changed since the signal: compare the results of limit orders with market ones in the order types below.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrderTypes_what: Trades grouped by the order type that opened them: market, limit (a level on the favourable side of price, below for a buy and above for a sell, with no slippage) and stop (a breakout level, with slippage). For each type: trades, average wait in candles until filled, win rate, profit factor, expectancy (average net P&L per trade) and slippage paid, on entry and exit.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrderTypes_read: A profit factor above 1 makes money; above 1.5 is good. If limit orders did much better than market ones, the edge lies in the entry price; if they did worse, it may be adverse selection (they only fill when price keeps going against). Slippage paid shows how much each type loses to execution; compare with the costs in 1.1.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrderTypes_cons:
Types mix different entries: the result may come from the entry, not the order.
With few trades in a type, the numbers are unreliable.
Limit fills are optimistic: a fill is assumed when the level is touched.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrderVariants_what: For each entry that enters at a level, the strategy re-run in the engine with only that entry's order changed: 1 candle without tracking, twice the candles, cancel or not without the condition (only with more than 1 candle) and at market. The current row is marked. Trades, filled and dropped (expired plus cancelled) belong to that entry; return and Δ (in p.p., against the current one) are for the whole strategy.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrderVariants_read: A positive Δ means the variant would have earned more than the current order. If the market version earns more, the level is losing good trades; if it loses a lot, the level is an important part of the edge. Small differences between variants are good: the strategy does not depend on fine-tuning the order. Large differences call for caution, because real execution is never the same as simulated.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrderVariants_pros:
Tests real alternatives to the order with the engine, not estimates.
Shows whether the order choice is robust or fragile.
Includes the comparison with entering at market, the simplest benchmark.
trading.fsExplain_setupOrderVariants_cons:
Only tests a few fixed variants, not every combination.
Picking the best variant from this table is optimising on the past; confirm out of sample (3.1).
Return is for the whole strategy, so knock-on changes in other entries (capital, positions) also feed into the Δ.
trading.fsExplain_setupRules_what: The indicators defined in the strategy (type, period, source, timeframe, shift and the RSI average, if any) and the general rules that were switched on: maximum positions, what to do on an opposite signal, position size and whether profits compound, size rules after streaks, broker minimums, the pause after an exit, excluded periods, blocked times, daily limits and the «do not trade if» rules.
trading.fsExplain_setupRules_read: Confirm the indicators and rules are the ones meant to be tested. Each rule switched on here later shows up as a blocking reason in the funnel (2.2): if a rule seems to have no effect or blocks too much, that is where it shows. Many rules with very precise values are a warning sign of overfitting; 3.4 (parameter sensitivity) tells whether those values survive small changes.
trading.fsExplain_sumBuyHold_what: The result of simply buying the asset and never selling: it buys with the initial capital at the start of the period and with each deposit when it comes in, pays the entry fee and values everything at the last price of the period. As a % of money put in, to compare directly with the net return.
trading.fsExplain_sumBuyHold_read: It is the minimum benchmark: if the strategy returns less than buy & hold, trading added no return (though it may have reduced risk, see max drawdown and 1.6). In a strong bull market it is hard to beat; in a sideways or falling market, a strategy that merely stays near 0 may already be better. Section 1.3 by horizon shows the comparison over several windows.
trading.fsExplain_sumBuyHold_cons:
It is a long-only benchmark: for strategies that short or stay out a lot, compare risk too.
Pays no exit fee or funding and has no capped drawdown: matching the return with a much smaller drop is also a good result.
Depends heavily on the period's start and end points.
trading.fsExplain_sumCapture_what: The strategy against the simulation's own asset, on UTC daily returns of the performance index and of price: up capture (strategy mean on days the asset rose ÷ asset mean on those days), down capture (the same on days it fell), beta (covariance ÷ asset variance), annual alpha ((mean − beta × asset mean) × 365), correlation and batting average (% of days the strategy did better than the asset).
trading.fsExplain_sumCapture_read: Ideal is high up capture and low (or negative) down capture: catch the rallies and protect in the drops. Beta near 1 and high correlation mean the strategy is almost the asset; beta near 0, that it is independent of it. A positive alpha is return beta does not explain. The scatter next to it shows the same days, point by point.
trading.fsExplain_sumCapture_pros:
Separates return from asset exposure from return due to the strategy.
Shows whether the strategy protects in drops, which total return does not tell.
trading.fsExplain_sumCapture_cons:
Measured against a single asset; strategies that short or stay out a lot give values that are hard to compare.
Up and down capture averages are unstable when the asset barely moves.
Batting average is low for strategies often out of the market (0% days against a rising asset).
trading.fsExplain_sumConclusions_what: The conclusions the simulator draws from this screen's numbers, one per line with a tone: favourable (+), unfavourable (−) or neutral (·). In Entries and exits: the best entry's share of profit, entries that flip sign out of sample, the return without the worst entry and the % of stops that later reached the target. In Hours: whether any time filter helped both in and out of sample, weekend versus week, working hours and session rules that improve results.
trading.fsExplain_sumConclusions_read: They are a starting point: each conclusion points to the block on the screen with the detail. Negative ones deserve attention first (e.g. an entry contributing over 100% of profit means the others lose). A positive suggestion (dropping an entry, a time filter) should be confirmed out of sample before applying it, to avoid overfitting.
trading.fsExplain_sumCosts_what: Everything trades paid over the period, in the quote currency: entry and exit fees, slippage (the price difference on market orders, stops and forced closes) and funding on perpetual futures. It is already deducted from P&L and final capital.
trading.fsExplain_sumCosts_read: Compare it with gross profit: if costs eat a large share of it, the strategy is fragile (the strategy score gives 0 for this part when costs reach 60% of gross profit). See what happens with double or triple fees in 3.5 and the monthly breakdown in the advanced view of 1.3.
trading.fsExplain_sumCvar95_what: Conditional VaR at 95% (expected shortfall): the average of the performance index's daily returns on days at or below VaR 95, i.e. the worst 5% of days.
trading.fsExplain_sumCvar95_read: It is the average loss when the day is truly bad. Compare it with VaR 95: if CVaR is much worse than VaR, extreme losses are large and the tail is fat. A CVaR of −4% means that on the worst days the capital loses 4% on average.
trading.fsExplain_sumCvar95_pros:
Captures the size of extreme losses, which VaR ignores.
More stable and informative than VaR for tail risk.
trading.fsExplain_sumCvar95_cons:
Based on few days (5% of the sample): very unstable with a short history.
Still historical: a never-seen crash is not included.
Days without a position also soften it.
trading.fsExplain_sumDistribution_what: A histogram of the performance index's daily returns (without deposits), in 41 bars symmetric around 0, up to the largest absolute return (at most 6 standard deviations; anything beyond counts in the end bars). The line shows how many days a normal distribution with the same mean and deviation would give.
trading.fsExplain_sumDistribution_read: End bars above the line are fat tails: extreme days happen more often than the normal predicts, and Sharpe and VaR understate the risk. A right tail longer than the left is desirable (positive skew). A huge spike at 0 comes from days without a position. Compare with skewness and kurtosis in 1.4.
trading.fsExplain_sumDistribution_pros:
Shows the real shape of risk, not just mean and deviation.
Reveals at a glance whether the strategy has hidden extreme losses.
trading.fsExplain_sumDistribution_cons:
Ignores the order of days (losing streaks do not show).
Days out of the market pile up at 0 and distort the shape.
With few days, the bars are jagged and hard to read.
trading.fsExplain_sumDrawdownCount_what: How many times the performance index (without deposits) fell below its previous high. Each episode runs from the day of the high until the day it is regained, or until the end of the period if not yet.
trading.fsExplain_sumDrawdownCount_read: Many short, shallow episodes are normal and healthy; a few very long ones are worse. The count only tells frequency: see each episode's depth and duration in the drawdown table just below and the time underwater in 1.2.
trading.fsExplain_sumDrawdownEpisodes_what: Every drawdown episode of the performance index (without deposits), deepest first: the start (the day of the high), the trough, the recovery (the day the high is regained, or «ongoing»), the depth in % and the days to trough, to recover and in total. The screen shows 5; «See all» opens the full list full screen.
trading.fsExplain_sumDrawdownEpisodes_read: Look at the top ones: how much it fell and, above all, how long it took to recover. Recoveries much longer than the drops point to a strategy that loses fast and gains slowly. An «ongoing» episode at the end may mean the strategy stopped working. Cross the dates with 1.3 and the regimes in 3.6.
trading.fsExplain_sumEquity_what: The strategy's capital on each UTC day (open positions at the end-of-day price, deposits included) versus buy & hold capital with the same deposits and entry fee. On a log scale, so the same % takes the same space at any height. At the bottom, as an orange area with its own scale, the strategy's drawdown (distance from the performance index's high).
trading.fsExplain_sumEquity_read: A good curve rises steadily, without huge steps or long flat stretches. If the buy & hold line is almost always above, the strategy added no return. Look at which phases it wins and loses in (trend, sideways, falling) and confirm with the regimes in 3.6. The drawdown area shows when and how much it hurt.
trading.fsExplain_sumEquity_cons:
It is a single history: the future will not repeat this sequence (see the Monte Carlo in 3.2).
With deposits, the capital line also rises from money put in; the drawdown already excludes it.
Daily points hide what happens within the day.
trading.fsExplain_sumEquityBase_what: Each day's capital divided by the asset's price at that moment: how much of the asset (e.g. how many BTC) the strategy's capital would buy. The last point uses the closing price of the period. Shows the initial and final quantity.
trading.fsExplain_sumEquityBase_read: If the line rises, the strategy beats the asset itself; if it falls while the capital in the quote currency rises, it earns less than buying and holding. It is the right view for someone who wants to accumulate the asset: a strategy that sells into drops and buys back cheaper pushes this curve up.
trading.fsExplain_sumEquityBase_cons:
Includes deposits (which also buy units), so it is not a pure performance measure.
In falling markets it can rise even though the strategy loses money in the quote currency.
Ignores the fee it would cost to convert back into the asset.
trading.fsExplain_sumFinalCapital_what: The capital the simulation ends with, in the quote currency, after every position is closed (the end of the period closes any still open). It includes the initial capital, the deposits and the net result of all trades, with fees, slippage and funding already taken off.
trading.fsExplain_sumFinalCapital_read: Compare it with the initial capital and deposits shown below: only the difference is profit. With deposits, a high final capital may come mostly from money put in, so the net return and CAGR next to it say more. Check it against buy & hold (the card next to it and 1.2) to see whether trading was worth it.
trading.fsExplain_sumHorizons_what: For the last 1, 3 and 6 months and 1, 3 and 5 years before the end (only those that fit in the period) and for the whole period: the strategy's return on the performance index (without deposits), buy & hold on price with the entry fee, the difference in percentage points, the strategy's largest drop within the window and the trades closed in it.
trading.fsExplain_sumHorizons_read: Shows whether the strategy still works in the recent past or whether the result comes entirely from older years. A positive difference across all horizons is a good sign; if short horizons are negative and the total very positive, the edge may be fading (confirm with the rolling Sharpe and 3.3).
trading.fsExplain_sumHorizons_cons:
Short horizons have few trades and a lot of noise.
They all end on the same day: an unusual period end affects them all.
Buy & hold here excludes deposits, unlike the 1.1 card.
trading.fsExplain_sumKurtosis_what: The excess kurtosis of the performance index's daily returns: the fourth central moment over the deviation to the fourth, minus 3. The normal has 0; above 0, extreme days (either way) appear more often than in a normal.
trading.fsExplain_sumKurtosis_read: Values above 3 indicate fat tails: Sharpe, volatility and VaR understate the real risk. High values are common in crypto. Read it with skewness: high kurtosis with negative skew is the worst case (rare extreme losses); with positive skew, extremes tend to be gains.
trading.fsExplain_sumKurtosis_pros:
Warns when deviation-based measures mislead.
Easy to compare with the normal's reference (0).
trading.fsExplain_sumKurtosis_cons:
Dominated by a handful of extreme days.
Does not say whether extremes are gains or losses.
Many 0% days out of the market inflate it artificially.
trading.fsExplain_sumMaxDrawdown_what: The largest drop, in %, from a capital peak to the following trough, measured day by day on the performance index (open positions at the end of each UTC day, without the effect of deposits). Calmar, below, is the CAGR divided by this drop.
trading.fsExplain_sumMaxDrawdown_read: It is the worst loss someone who started at the worst moment would have suffered. Below 20% is comfortable for most; above 30–40% is hard to stomach in practice, even with a good final return. A Calmar above 1 means the annual gain exceeds the worst drop. See duration and recovery in the episodes in 1.4 and what is realistic to expect in the Monte Carlo in 3.2.
trading.fsExplain_sumMaxDrawdown_pros:
Measures risk the way it is felt: the largest loss from a high.
Easy to compare with personal tolerance and with prop firm rules.
trading.fsExplain_sumMaxDrawdown_cons:
It is a single episode: history may have been lucky and the next one larger (see 3.2).
Measured on daily closes: intraday drops and recoveries do not show, so the intraday loss may have been bigger.
Does not say how long the capital stayed below the peak (see 1.2 underwater).
trading.fsExplain_sumMonthlyDetail_what: One row per UTC month: trades closed that month, win rate, stops (including trailing, break-even and liquidation) and take profits, gross P&L (before fees and funding; slippage is already in the prices), fees, funding, net P&L, the month's return and largest drop on the performance index (open positions included, no deposits) and end-of-month capital (with deposits).
trading.fsExplain_sumMonthlyDetail_read: It explains each month: a bad month with many stops is different from a bad month due to costs or funding. Compare gross and net P&L to see the weight of costs. The return may not match the net P&L, because it includes positions still open at month end and P&L is counted by exit month.
trading.fsExplain_sumNetReturn_what: Net profit (final capital minus initial capital and deposits) as a % of everything put in, with the same profit in money and the CAGR below. CAGR is the compound annual return, computed on the performance index (which removes the effect of deposits) over the period length in years of 365.25 days.
trading.fsExplain_sumNetReturn_read: Positive means profit, but what matters is how it compares with buy & hold and with the risk taken (max drawdown, volatility). CAGR lets simulations of different lengths be compared: 100% over 5 years is a CAGR of about 15%. A very high CAGR over a short span is usually unstable; confirm it in 1.3 by horizon and in 3.1 out of sample.
trading.fsExplain_sumNetReturn_cons:
With deposits, the return on money put in and the index CAGR can differ a lot.
Over short periods CAGR exaggerates: a few good months annualised look extraordinary.
Ignores the risk taken to get there.
trading.fsExplain_sumPain_what: The Pain index: the mean of daily drawdowns, in %, on the performance index (without deposits). It tells how far, on average, equity sat below its previous peak over the whole period.
trading.fsExplain_sumPain_read: Lower is better. It is similar to the Ulcer but linear: every drop counts by its depth, without extra weight for deep ones. If the Ulcer is much larger than the Pain, there are a few deep drops; if they are close, losses are shallow and frequent.
trading.fsExplain_sumPain_pros:
Easy to interpret: the average loss from the peak.
Counts every day below the high, not only the worst.
trading.fsExplain_sumPain_cons:
Does not highlight deep drops, which are the dangerous ones.
Measured on daily closes.
Depends on the period's starting point.
trading.fsExplain_sumPositiveDays_what: The % of UTC days on which the performance index rose (without the effect of deposits), out of all days in the period. Days with no position and no movement count as not positive.
trading.fsExplain_sumPositiveDays_read: Tells how often equity goes up: a trend strategy may have only 30–40% positive days and still earn a lot on the few good ones. Read it alongside time in market: with little exposure the % is naturally low. The calendar in 5.5 shows positive and negative days one by one.
trading.fsExplain_sumPositiveDays_cons:
Penalised by days out of the market, which are not bad days.
Does not show how big the good and bad days are (see the distribution in 1.3 and the best and worst day in 1.4).
trading.fsExplain_sumProfitFactor_what: Profit factor is the sum of net P&L of winning trades divided by the absolute sum of losing trades. Below, the expectancy: the average net P&L per trade, in the quote currency.
trading.fsExplain_sumProfitFactor_read: Below 1 the strategy loses; 1.3 is good, above 1.6 very good, and above 3 with many trades is rare and should be confirmed out of sample (3.1). Expectancy tells how much each trade earns on average: compare it with the cost per trade to see the margin. With no losing trade, profit factor is left empty.
trading.fsExplain_sumProfitFactor_pros:
Sums up in one number the balance between what is won and lost, costs included.
Independent of trade order and easy to compare across strategies.
trading.fsExplain_sumProfitFactor_cons:
A single huge trade can push it way up.
Ignores time and capital used: two systems with the same PF can have very different drawdowns.
Expectancy in money depends on position size; to compare entries, use R (4.1).
trading.fsExplain_sumRatios_what: The main return-to-risk ratios, each with its value, the buy & hold value (where it exists), formula, reference and reading: Sharpe, Sortino and Calmar (as in the cards, on the performance index, and for buy & hold on the daily price); Omega (sum of positive days over sum of negative days); Gain-to-Pain (sum of monthly returns over sum of monthly losses); profit factor; SQN (√n × mean ÷ deviation of each trade's return on capital, n capped at 100); and Kelly (W − (1 − W) ÷ payoff).
trading.fsExplain_sumRatios_read: The «Reading» column rates each ratio by the levels shown in the reference (weak, good, very good, excellent; for Kelly, whether there is an edge). More important than any single ratio is consistency: if all say «good», the result is coherent; if Sharpe is good but Omega and Gain-to-Pain are weak, look at the distribution. Compare with buy & hold to see whether the risk was well used.
trading.fsExplain_sumRatios_pros:
Several angles on the same problem: volatility, drawdowns, tails, trades and bet size.
Each row carries its formula and reference, no need to look them up.
trading.fsExplain_sumRatios_cons:
Reference levels are general conventions, not asset-specific.
They all measure the same history: excellent ratios on an optimised backtest are suspect.
Full Kelly is aggressive: in practice a fraction is used (see 4.6).
trading.fsExplain_sumReturns_what: A heatmap with the % return of each month, quarter or year (UTC; chosen at the top), computed on the performance index (without deposits): the value at the end of the period over the value at the start. The last column is the year. Blue for gains, orange for losses, on a symmetric scale up to the largest month or quarter in the view; periods the simulation only partly covers are dashed.
trading.fsExplain_sumReturns_read: Look for consistency: many small blue months beat one or two huge months that pay for everything. See whether losses cluster in certain years or seasons and whether recent years are worse than older ones (a sign the edge is fading). The colour legend filters periods by return range. «Advanced view» shows each month in detail.
trading.fsExplain_sumReturns_cons:
Calendar months and quarters are arbitrary cuts: a bad stretch across two months gets diluted.
Partial periods (first and last) are not comparable with full ones.
Does not show the risk inside each period (see the advanced view).
trading.fsExplain_sumRollingSharpe_what: On each day, the Sharpe of the last 60 daily returns of the performance index (without deposits), annualised with √365. When there is no movement in the window (no positions), there is no Sharpe and the line breaks. Reference lines sit at 0, 1 and 2.
trading.fsExplain_sumRollingSharpe_read: Shows whether performance is steady or comes from a few phases: a line that spends most of the time above 1 is solid. A persistent fall below 0 at the end of the period is the first sign the edge may be fading. Compare with the regimes in 3.6 to see in which market conditions the Sharpe drops.
trading.fsExplain_sumRollingSharpe_pros:
Reveals instability that the overall Sharpe hides.
Shows when the strategy stopped working.
trading.fsExplain_sumRollingSharpe_cons:
60 days is a short window: values swing a lot and extremes of ±5 are common.
Windows with few trades give misleading Sharpes.
Consecutive days share almost the whole window, so the values are not independent.
trading.fsExplain_sumScatter_what: One point per UTC day: the asset's return on the horizontal axis, the strategy's (performance index, without deposits) on the vertical. The line is the least-squares fit and its slope is the beta. Both axes share the same symmetric scale, up to the largest absolute daily return.
trading.fsExplain_sumScatter_read: A cloud stretched along a sloped line means the strategy follows the asset; a flat cloud near the horizontal axis means it barely depends on it. Points in the top-left quadrant (asset fell, strategy gained) are days it protected or profited from the drop. Many points on the horizontal axis are days without a position.
trading.fsExplain_sumScatter_pros:
Shows the relation with the asset day by day, not just in summary numbers.
Reveals anomalous days and asymmetries between rallies and drops.
trading.fsExplain_sumScatter_cons:
The line is heavily influenced by a few extreme days.
Days out of the market (0%) pile up and pull the beta towards 0.
Ignores the order and timing of days.
trading.fsExplain_sumScore_what: A score from 0 to 100 combining six parts, each a fraction from 0 to 1 times its weight: profitability 25 (Sharpe and CAGR), risk 20 (max drawdown and volatility), out of sample 20 (return and profit factor out versus in; with no split set, the last 30%), significance 15 (number of trades and the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio), stability 10 (R² of a line fitted to the log of equity) and costs 10 (costs over gross profit). «How the score is calculated» shows the maths with this simulation's numbers.
trading.fsExplain_sumScore_read: 70 or more is «solid», 45 to 69 «promising, with reservations» and below 45 «not ready yet». More than the total, look at the bars: an orange part points to the weakness (e.g. low significance = few trades). Confirm with the verdict and the Proofs (screen 3), which test robustness more thoroughly.
trading.fsExplain_sumScore_pros:
Sums up in one number several dimensions no single indicator captures.
Transparent: each part shows its formula and the numbers used.
Prioritises robustness and significance, not just return.
trading.fsExplain_sumScore_cons:
Scales and weights are conventions, not a statistical truth.
A high score does not guarantee future results: it is still measured on the same history.
Parts can offset each other and hide a serious problem in one of them.
trading.fsExplain_sumSharpe_what: Sharpe is the mean of daily returns divided by their standard deviation, annualised with √365 (crypto never closes) and with no risk-free rate. It is computed on the performance index, with open positions valued at the end of each UTC day and without the effect of deposits. Sortino, below, uses only the volatility of losing days in the denominator.
trading.fsExplain_sumSharpe_read: Below 0 the strategy loses; between 0 and 1 the return barely pays for the volatility; above 1 is good, above 2 very good, and above 3 in a backtest deserves suspicion (overfitting or a short sample). A Sortino well above Sharpe means the volatility is mostly upside. See how it evolves in the rolling Sharpe in 1.3 and compare with buy & hold in 1.5.
trading.fsExplain_sumSharpe_pros:
The standard measure of return per unit of risk, comparable across strategies and assets.
Computed day by day on equity including open positions, not just on closed trades.
trading.fsExplain_sumSharpe_cons:
Treats upside volatility as risk; Sortino fixes that.
Assumes roughly normal returns: fat tails (see 1.4) make it look better than it is.
Days without a position count as 0%, which lowers the deviation and can inflate the Sharpe of strategies that trade rarely.
trading.fsExplain_sumSkewness_what: The skewness of the performance index's daily returns: the third central moment over the cubed deviation. 0 is symmetric; negative means big drops are more frequent or larger than big gains; positive, the opposite.
trading.fsExplain_sumSkewness_read: Positive is desirable: many small losses and a few big wins, typical of trend strategies with a stop. Negative is the «picking up pennies in front of a steamroller» profile: small, regular gains and now and then a big loss (common in mean reversion and selling volatility). See the shape in the 1.3 distribution.
trading.fsExplain_sumSkewness_pros:
Reveals risks the Sharpe and volatility do not show.
Helps identify the type of strategy and its typical danger.
trading.fsExplain_sumSkewness_cons:
Very sensitive to one or two extreme days.
With few days, the value is unreliable.
Days without a position (0%) change it.
trading.fsExplain_sumTailRatio_what: The tail ratio: the 95th percentile of the performance index's daily returns divided by the absolute 5th percentile. It compares the size of very good days with very bad ones.
trading.fsExplain_sumTailRatio_read: Above 1, the best 5% of days are larger than the worst 5%: a good sign, especially for trend strategies. Below 1, extreme losses outweigh extreme gains. It is empty if the 5th percentile is not negative. Read it with skewness and the 1.3 distribution.
trading.fsExplain_sumTailRatio_pros:
Intuitive: compares the two tails directly.
Less sensitive to a single extreme day than skewness.
trading.fsExplain_sumTailRatio_cons:
Ignores what happens beyond the 5th and 95th percentiles.
0% days out of the market can shift the percentiles.
Unstable with few days.
trading.fsExplain_sumTimeInMarket_what: The % of the period with at least one open position, merging trades without counting twice the time when several were open together. Below, the most positions open at the same time.
trading.fsExplain_sumTimeInMarket_read: Little time in the market with a good return is efficient: capital stays free and exposed to fewer risks (gaps, news). Near 100% the strategy behaves almost like being always positioned and should be compared closely with buy & hold. The maximum positions shows the peak exposure that pyramiding or several entries reached.
trading.fsExplain_sumTimeInMarket_cons:
Says nothing about position size: 10% of the time at high leverage can be risky.
Ignores the direction (long or short) of the exposure.
trading.fsExplain_sumTrades_what: The number of trades closed in the period (the end of the period closes any still open) and, below, the monthly average. A trade is the whole position, even if it had partial exits or scale-ins.
trading.fsExplain_sumTrades_read: It is the sample size: with fewer than 30 trades the report's numbers are unreliable and the verdict stays inconclusive; from 100 the sample test passes. Many trades per month with a small average profit make the strategy sensitive to costs (see 3.5). Compare with the signal funnel in 2.2 to see how many signals went unused.
trading.fsExplain_sumUlcer_what: The Ulcer index: the square root of the mean of squared daily drawdowns, in %, on the performance index (without deposits). It combines in one number how deep and how long equity stayed below its previous peak, weighting deep drops more.
trading.fsExplain_sumUlcer_read: Lower is better: below 5% is calm, above 15% is a strategy that spends a lot of time in significant losses. Unlike max drawdown, it counts every day, not just the worst episode. Use it to compare strategies with similar returns: the one with the lower Ulcer is easier to stick with.
trading.fsExplain_sumUlcer_pros:
Measures the stress of being in a loss, not just the worst moment.
Penalises deep drops more than shallow ones.
trading.fsExplain_sumUlcer_cons:
A long shallow drop and a short deep one can give the same value.
Measured on daily closes.
Less known, with fewer benchmarks than drawdown.
trading.fsExplain_sumUnderwater_what: For each day, the % distance of the performance index (without deposits) from its previous high: 0 at a new high, negative below it. It also shows the largest drop and the longest stretch, in days, from a high until it is regained (or the end, if not yet).
trading.fsExplain_sumUnderwater_read: Look at both depth and duration: a strategy that spends months or years underwater is hard to stick with, even with a good final return. Many quick returns to 0 are a good sign. Compare with the episodes in 1.4 and with the Ulcer and Pain index, which sum this curve up in one number.
trading.fsExplain_sumUnderwater_pros:
Shows the pain of holding the strategy: how much and for how long it was below the high.
Reveals long stagnation that the equity curve hides.
trading.fsExplain_sumUnderwater_cons:
Based on daily closes: intraday drops do not show.
Depends on the starting point: starting after a high changes everything.
It is one historical sequence; another order of the same days would give another curve (see 3.2).
trading.fsExplain_sumVar95_what: Value at Risk at 95%: the 5th percentile of the performance index's daily returns (without deposits), in %. Only 5% of days, one in 20, ended below this value.
trading.fsExplain_sumVar95_read: Tells how much can be lost on a bad but ordinary day: with a VaR 95 of −2%, roughly one day a month loses 2% or more. Compare with CVaR 95, the average loss on those days, and with VaR 99. Small values may simply come from lots of time out of the market.
trading.fsExplain_sumVar95_pros:
A standard risk measure, easy to turn into money for the account size.
Historical: does not assume a normal distribution.
trading.fsExplain_sumVar95_cons:
Says nothing about what happens beyond the threshold (that is CVaR).
Days without a position, at 0%, push it up and hide the risk while positioned.
Measured on daily closes; the intraday loss may have been larger.
trading.fsExplain_sumVar99_what: Value at Risk at 99%: the 1st percentile of the performance index's daily returns (without deposits). Only 1% of days, one in 100, ended below this value.
trading.fsExplain_sumVar99_read: It is the very bad day that happens a few times a year. Compare with VaR 95: if VaR 99 is several times worse, risk is concentrated in a few extreme days. Use it to think about position size and the leverage that can survive such a day.
trading.fsExplain_sumVar99_pros:
Looks further into the tail than VaR 95.
Useful for sizing leverage and daily loss rules.
trading.fsExplain_sumVar99_cons:
Rests on very few days: with a year of data, 3 or 4.
Does not say how big losses beyond it are.
Very sensitive to a single extreme event in the history.
trading.fsExplain_sumVerdict_what: The verdict combines the robustness tests from the Proofs (screen 3) and the sample: sample size (100 trades passes, under 30 fails), out of sample (3.1, positive annualised return out of sample), Monte Carlo (3.2, under 20% of paths losing passes, over 40% fails), parameter sensitivity (3.4, 80% of variants profitable passes, under 50% fails), walk-forward (3.3), costs (3.5, profitable with doubled fees), market regimes (3.6) and concentration (the 5 best days are at most 50% of profit). Each passes, fails or is undecided.
trading.fsExplain_sumVerdict_read: «Robust» means no test fails and at least 5 pass; «fragile», 3 or more fail; the rest, or anything with fewer than 30 trades, is «inconclusive». Read the failing tests first: each line gives the number behind the decision and where to see the detail. A fragile strategy can have a great return, but it depends on the period, the parameters or a few days.
trading.fsExplain_sumVerdict_pros:
Puts in one place what the report says about trust in the result.
